subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under Standing Order 52 and pursuant to the notice which the Chair received earlier this morning and which it now has, I would like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception, that this House engage in an emergency debate on the escalating crisis in Yugoslavia.
Very briefly, Dubrovnik in the last 36 hours has come under heavy artillery rocket fire attack by the Yugoslav army and navy. The bombing has caused extensive damage to the centre of that city, the ancient medieval city known as the Pearl of the Adriatic. It marks the first destruction of that old city despite the fact that it was established in the 14th century, survived the Turkish expansion and two world wars. The attacks seem to be intensifying hourly, according to my information.
The old walled city has been recognized by UNESCO as a class o cultural monument of world international importance along with things like the pyramids. In a less vicious way the city has been under siege for the past 25 days. I understand there are presently over 65,000 civilians taking refuge within its walls. It has been under bombardment by land, air and sea, as I have said, for 36 hours. I would point out that the Yugoslav army became a signatory to international law in 1955, a law that requires the protection of cultural historic monuments of world importance and significance.
All this is happening 24 hours after the Yugoslav army general flatly rejected participation by the European community brokered peace plan. At the same time the army, as I understand it, condoned a mobilization of reservists in an all-out offensive on the democratic republic of Croatia.
In those indicated circumstances, especially given what has happened in the past 36 hours, I would ask that the Chair consider under Standing Order 52 the granting of an emergency debate.

October 24, 1991

He said: Madam Speaker, today we will be asking the Chair to permit us to reduce the time of our speeches on this side of the House to 10 minutes each, followed by a 5-minute question and answer period. A lot of members on this side want to express their opinions and lay upon the table of the House the facts regarding transfer and equalization payments from the federal government to the four provincial governments in Atlantic Canada.
Our chairman of the Atlantic caucus, the hon. member for Dartmouth will in a few moments outline our main concerns with government policy. Later the hon. member for Burin-St. George's will outline as well the problems we are having with transfer payments, the fishery and other things of major concern to the province of Newfoundland.
One of our colleagues from New Brunswick will outline the substantial reduction in transfer payments. The news has quoted a $100 million reduction to the province of New Brunswick.
Another colleague from Prince Edward Island will be able to lay on the table of this House the most recent figures on transfer payments.
My colleague from Prince Edward Island will be able to show that there has been a substantial reduction in the equalization payments from the federal government to certain provincial governments in Atlantic Canada. This is according to figures from the federal Department of Finance that were given to members of Parliament just a couple of days ago. In other words, they are up-to-date figures for October of this year. We are requesting, Madam Speaker, that you recognize us for 10 minutes at a time so that we can present the case as strongly as possible to the Canadian people and to the Government of Canada that they need a major policy change.
The major point that I want to make in introducing the debate relates, as our motion says, to the destructive policies of the Government of Canada toward our major industries. One of my colleagues from Cape Breton Island will be speaking later in this debate and showing how the sale of the railway by the Government of Canada is threatening a forest products industry on Cape Breton Island located in Port Hawkesbury. He will present to the House the facts of the potential loss of hundreds and hundreds of jobs.
I have two pieces of paper in my hand. One is a news release by the Government of Canada issued two days ago and the other is a communication from the Soviet Union to a department of the federal government.
The press release that was issued just two days ago said that Canada has notified the Government of Japan of the approval of licences permitting seven Japanese vessels to fish a portion of Japan's international quota for blue fin tuna in Canadian division 3-0. Two days ago Canada notified the Government of Japan that seven of its fishing vessels can come inside our 200-mile zone this year and fish a portion of their international quota for tuna in competition with our Canadian fishermen.
Of course the reason why this was made in a news release was because it goes on to say that last year they allowed 16 vessels in from Japan. Then they go on in the news release and say that it was only five or six years ago that they allowed in 100 vessels. They brag about the fact that they are now allowing in only seven Japanese vessels. It is quite a statement to make because the quotas have not changed. You could allow in seven vessels 200-feet long and it is the same as 100 vessels 30-feet long.
October 24, 1991

The quotas for this year agreed to by the Canadian government stand at 1,300 tonnes to the U.S.A., 700 tonnes to Japan, and 550 tonnes to Canada for that fish stock. We are saying to our Canadian fishermen: "You cannot have any more licences. Your quota is frozen at 560 tonnes. You are not allowed to have any more licences but you can come and fish inside our 200-mile zone in 1992 while our fishery is in such disarray".
I went over the figures for before coming here today with the department. They showed that last year Japan not only caught its blue fin tuna inside our 200-mile zone but it caught unlimited amounts of albacore tuna, swordfish, big-eyed tuna, yellow fin tuna: unlimited quotas for big eye and yellow fin. We say to the Government of Canada: "Open your big eye. Forget your yellow fin and kick them out".

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is not with a great deal of pleasure that I speak in this debate today. I believed when I first got elected here that the Government of Canada had a responsibility to govern all of the citizens of the country with fairness and equity in mind. It is becoming increasingly apparent, particularly over the last few days, that that sense of fairness, equality and duty are no longer there.
I would like to try to give some indication to the House and to those people who are watching exactly why we in the Atlantic, a vital part of this country, absolutely condemn and reject this government's economic policies. It has amounted to nothing short of an absolute assault and battery on each and every individual Canadian that is living in any region of this country outside of the have provinces, but most particularly those that live in the region of Atlantic Canada.
Back in 1988 when the government came into power it tried to cleanse its record of neglect in dealing with Atlantic Canadian economic issues. Just prior to that, in 1987, the Prime Minister made a major announcement saying that his government, as it was constitutionally bound to be, was in support of the principle of equalization, and the way that they were going to pursue their program of equalization was clearly going to be with a new program. I am going to quote the Prime Minister when he announced the $1.05 billion which was going to be the panacea for the economic ills of Atlantic Canada. He announced the creation of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and he said: "We begin with new money, a new mission, and a new opportunity".
My, my, my, Madam Speaker, just a few years later how those words ring hollow.
The facts, which I am going to present, will show very clearly that this government and the statements of the Prime Minister back in 1987 have been absolutely contradicted by its actions.
The reason we are debating this today is that just a few days ago the provincial premiers in Atlantic Canada found that because of a quirk or a change or a formula that was kicking in in the equalization program, the amount of money they expected to get this current year would be diminished by over $170 million. It is not $170,000, but $170 million to Canada's poorest region, a place where there are only 2.2 million or 2.3 million people.
I want to make everyone aware of what equalization is. It is an unconditional-I want to underline that-an unconditional transfer to the provinces. What is it there for? It is there to ensure that the constitutional requirement that Canadians no matter where they live have a right to expect programs of a national standard are able to be maintained. That is what it is there for. In
October 24, 1991

provinces like Newfoundland where the unemployment rate is 70 per cent above the national average; in Prince Edward Island where the per capita income is 32 per cent less than the national average, the government, the Minister of Finance's own press secretary two days ago came out and said: "It is $170 million in cuts, so what. We've got $170 million in cuts because the economies are performing so well in Atlantic Canada". What utter nonsense and what arrogance.
Tell that to the fisherman who is going to face a winter on welfare, if he can get welfare from nearly bankrupt municipalities in Atlantic Canada. Tell that to the people who are waiting for hospital beds in parts of Atlantic Canada because the provincial government's do not have the fiscal ability any more with the cuts that have taken place to provide quality health care of national standards. Tell that to the students who because of rising tuitions and no job opportunities in Atlantic Canada cannot pursue their post-secondary education.
This government has struck at the very heart of what this country is all about in its crazy attempt to impose its fiscal regime and straitjacket on all Canadians.
It was Liberal governments which put in these programs that believed in the principle of equality and fairness, that believed in equalization and sought and got it put right into our Constitution in 1982. It is part of our Constitution. It is not part of some other piece of legislation that can be easily amended or changed by a majority in this place. National standards are part of our Constitution.
Previous Liberal governments believed it was important to redistribute wealth not just through equalization but through a process called economic regional development agreements whereby the federal government became a partner in the poorest provinces in this country in putting forward programs in fisheries development, quality enhancement, not just welfare payments. Money was put into programs to ensure that our fisheries was more efficient. Money was put into our forestry for silviculture so that it truly was a renewable resource. Money was put into special manpower training and mineral development and mineral exploration agreements because it was a real attempt-which was starting to work-to make sure that those regions were have regions, not just regions that constantly were on their

knees begging a benevolent Ontario for more money. That was the principle.
Between 1984 and 1989 there was $114 million worth of agreements. I am wrong, $1,144 billion worth of agreements that expired, in 1984 dollars. They provided tens of thousands of jobs in Atlantic Canada. What did this government do? Did it do the right thing? Did it go back in and renew those agreements? Maybe it did. It provided $272 million which would be the equivalent to probably about $150 million, 10 per cent, almost, which is a 90 per cent reduction in funding available for regional development agreements. That has caused us a crippling blow in Atlantic Canada.
In addition to that it came out with freezes on EPFs. That is transfers to the provinces for Established Programs Financing, programs in health care and programs in post-secondary education, which is a little different from equalization. These dollars are specifically to go to those provinces to ensure that the men, women and children who live in those provinces have programs of national standards in health care and programs of national standards in post-secondary education, a principle that this country was bom on and that it developed on.
What does this government do? It walks in and it cuts. Boy did it cut. It cut to the quick. For example, in little Prince Edward Island the effect of the freeze on any increase in EPFs, means this to every one of you people out there in P.E.I. Sixteen million dollars less will come in for hospitals and health care in P.E.I. this year, $7 million less will come in for post-secondary education. My goodness, there are only 130,000 odd souls in Prince Edward Island. Have you any idea what the effect of these callous and cold cuts in EPF are having on the ability of provincial governments to deliver those services with national standards?
In Nova Scotia, $111 million less will be transferred through EPFs to support health care. In Newfoundland, there will be $29 million less for post-secondary education. Do you wonder why we are standing in this House

today and saying that this government has gone absolutely against our very own Constitution here.
The government will tell you that regional disparity is not really a problem, that it has improved the relative standing of the Atlantic. I want to read this quickly: "In 1988, unemployment in Newfoundland was 53 per cent higher than the national average in 1982, but had increased to a level of 110 per cent higher as of 1988." That is a real measure of regional disparity. The regions in the Atlantic provinces are not closing the gap, the gap is getting bigger. Each time this government comes in with regressive, Draconian cuts, like it did yesterday or the day before, it gets worse.
I wish I had two days to speak on this, but I do not, I have about 30 seconds. I want to finish by quoting one thing here. I am quoting from the Constitution Act, Part III, Section 36 which is the mandate of the Government and the people of Canada. It states:
(a)	promoting equal opportunities for the well-being of
Canadians;
(b)	furthering economic development to reduce disparity in
opportunities; and
(c)	providing essential public services of reasonable quality to all
Canadians.
I submit to you, Madam Speaker, that what this government has done with the series of cuts that it has undertaken over the last two years has been tantamount to violating the Constitution of this country. What it has done is ensure that there are two classes of Canadians, those that have and those that have not. Unfortunately those have not mostly reside in Atlantic Canada. We will have no more of it.

He is an Atlantic Canadian and he knows full well that Atlantic Canada has been able to develop and prosper because of Liberal policies such as equalization and fiscal transfers. He knows that full well. He sits on the side of the government that has done everything in its power to dismantle those economic tools of nation building.
Madam Speaker, anybody who tries to tell you that a constitution has nothing to do with economies is crazy. If peoples' economic well being is looked after, they are probably going to be able to find accommodations and compromises on those other things that divide us and which are currently the subject of great debate across this country as to whether or not we can truly stay together.
As far as the comments by that great Liberal Clyde Wells are concerned, I am certain that Premier Wells is in a very difficult position. He is dealing with a federal government that has basically bankrupted the country because of its fiscal mismanagement. Clyde Wells probably tells the truth in this case. Clyde Wells says he can understand what is going on, because these members opposite, the government opposite, has virtually bankrupted the country.
Many would argue that we are no longer a viable, competitive force internationally because of the high dollar, high tax and high interest rate policy of this government. So I can understand Clyde Wells.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate because the motion and the comments that have been made in speaking to the motion are misleading and inaccurate. It gives me an opportunity to set the record straight.
The issue of the equalization recalculation is not a surprise. It is not a quirk. It is not a change in policy. It is a fact of life. It has been there for many years, since equalization has been in place. There are no surprises. All the provincial governments involved know this. Their officials have been well aware of this. This is a very normal occurrence. For hon. members to express outrage is totally erroneous and misleading and not in accordance with the facts.
I want to deal with three specific points in addressing this issue, Madam Speaker.
The first point is this. We are not slashing, we are not robbing and we are not massively reducing transfer payments. That is categorical. The fact is that we are increasing transfer payments. We have increased them enormously and we will continue to increase them. As a matter of fact, in 1984-85 total transfers to the provinces including cash and tax transfer points amounted to $25.6 billion. In 1992-93 the projections are $38.1 billion, which means there will be an increase over that period of time of $12.5 billion. Common sense and logic would tell you that that is not a reduction, that is an increase and that fact has to be made.
I could go through each and every one of the components that make this up. EPF, which we have heard so much about, Established Programs Financing which provides assistance to the provinces for health, welfare and education, in 1984-85, the figure was $14,568 billion. This year, the figure is $20,368 billion and in 1992-93, they will continue their rise and will reach $20,620 billion.
How these members can stand up in this House and condemn the government for reducing transfer payments and do it with a straight face is beyond me. I do not understand it. Surely, this is a time when we should have an honest debate. There has got to be some

The third point I want to make is that the best guarantee to preserve our health care and education system across the country is to renew economic growth and sustained recovery with price stability, but for that to happen we have got to identify and get at the root causes of our problems, and that is to bring interest rates down. Interest rates are the key to stimulating economic growth. In order to get interest rates down, you must bring inflation down and you must bring the growth of expenditures down. You must tackle the deficit and you must tackle inflation.
This government has done both. We are making progress on both fronts. We must make progress on both fronts if we are going to lead to a sustained economic recovery.
I am pleased over the fact that over the last six month period the annualized rate of inflation was 2.5 per cent. I think it is better than any of us ever expected. That is very fundamental and very important if we are going to achieve two goals, the goal of price stability and the continuing decline in interest rates.
Our interest rates have gone down by almost 600 basis points or 6 per cent since the high of May 1990. The deficit and the way in which we manage our fiscal affairs is very, very vital and integral to identifying and tackling this problem. We must continue along the program of government expenditure restraint. We must continue to ratchet down the deficit. Our plan is to bring the deficit down to a level somewhere in the order of $25 billion in the next fiscal year, and by 1994-95 we will be in a position, hopefully, where we will not have to continue to borrow to meet our essential needs. Just to refresh our memory, the equalization program is designed to enable the provincial governments to provide reasonably comparable public services at reasonably comparable levels of taxation. It is a vital example of our national spirit of equality and mutual support. As hon. members have pointed out it is enshrined in the
Constitution. We consider it to be very important. It is part of the sense of equality in giving Canadians equal opportunity and equal services across the country.
I repeat again equalization is not being cut. It has not been cut this year. It has not been cut last year and it is not going to be cut in the years ahead. In fact the entitlements of provinces for 1991-92 are expected to rise by $250 million over the last year's level, as I have said, for a total of $8.3 billion or $8.4 billion. It will be expected to increase to $9.48 billion in the year 1992-93.

We can talk until we are blue in the face, criticize the formula and criticize the legislation, but all that is happening here is that we are applying the legislation. It is a normal procedure. Equalization payments are provided to the eligible provinces in advance on the basis of the best guessed estimates and a preliminary set of standards, and as more accurate information becomes available these adjustments are made.
This process is well understood by the provinces. It happens twice a year, usually in February and October. Often it means in most cases that we have to make additional payments to the provinces. Other times it shows that they have been overpaid. For example, in 1982-83 the adjustments under the formula meant that Saskatchewan owed the federal government approximately $100 million. I simply wanted to put on the record the facts that are existent and to lay it out in such a way as to demonstrate to hon. members that there is not a surprise or something unusual happening here. It is a normal course of events.
I guess that could apply for any reason. In western Canada we have the Western Diversification Program which provides assistance to broadening the economic base. We have the Northern Ontario Development Program. We have a regional development program in Quebec. We have programs in Ontario, for example, DIP. All these are in addition to the transfer payments that we talk about. We then go to the Atlantic region where we have support for the fisheries industry. We have had contracts that have been released to the Halifax-Dartmouth industries for the building of new vessels and new mine sweepers. We had the largest contract ever awarded by the Government of Canada, the frigate contract, to Saint John Shipbuilding. We also have ACOA.
ACOA has been a success story. It was not a program devised by the Liberal Government of Canada. It was devised by this government. It was devised by the members who represent the Atlantic region. It has been a program that has worked very well because it involves community. It involves the grassroots. It involves small business. It has created jobs and new opportunities and has broadened the economic base.
I think that those are dollars well spent. Those are the kinds of programs that will lift Atlantic Canada out of the kind of situation that it has experienced for many years. Hopefully, rather than being a recipient province under equalization, it will be a contributing province. I think that would be the desire of all Atlantic Canadians and that would be the desire of Quebecers as well.
What we are doing here is providing grants through Established Programs Financing, through equalization, through the Canada Assistance Program, to provide some equality of service right across the board. In addition, we are attempting to provide for programs that will encourage the enterprise skills and the innovative skills to be developed clearly to create jobs in long-term economic activity and prolonged and durable sustainable growth.

If we move out of the golden horseshoe or out of parts of Alberta and parts of British Columbia the economies of this country are in serious trouble. These economic policies in the regions of Canada have failed. We need a government which will re-orient economic policies to address inequality, to address the diversity of opportunities across this country.
If we look around the world, for example at the Thatcher government in England or the Reagan and Bush regimes in the United States, we see enormous equalities that have built up as a result of the pursuit of neo-conservative economic policies which have failed. agreement, an obsession with competition and the role of private capital.
If we look at the regions of Canada and at Atlantic Canada we can see that private capital and competition harshly judge these areas. If instead of pursuing those objectives, the government put emphasis on reducing unemployment rates by 1 percentage point, it would increase economic activity in Atlantic Canada to over $700 million, 14 times as much as might be saved by reducing provincial trade barriers. incidences of welfare and so on, but basically a loss of hope.

In terms of employment, for example, the number of people working in those economies-in Newfoundland, between 1990 and 1991 there was a reduction of 3,500 people in the workforce, the same in Prince Edward Island, a province with a population of only 140,000-odd; almost a thousand less people working in Nova Scotia and 1,500 less working in New Brunswick.
Not only do we have a situation in which their economies are in desperate straits but they are getting worse. The only conclusion we can make from this is that federal economic policies are not working, if what those policies are doing is attempting to increase employment opportunities and economic activity in the region. Clearly also the provincial government's strategies are not working in those regions.
So we have economies which are in desperate straits in Atlantic Canada. People living in Atlantic Canada simply do not have the opportunities that people in other parts of the country have. On top of all of this, rather than assist the people in those provinces more, to have the opportunities needed to raise their families and work, we see new cuts to equalization payments. Premier Wells of Newfoundland said that when you list all of the attacks on Atlantic Canada by the federal government, these cuts to equalization payments constitute the straw that breaks the camel's back. In other words, the premiers of Atlantic Canada realize that they have been done a serious disservice by this federal government.
But in spite of all of this, in spite of the feelings of the premiers of Atlantic Canada, three Liberal premiers and one Conservative premier, in spite of Premier Wells saying that this cut to equalization payments was the straw that broke the camel's back, let us look at what the premiers said in response to what they called "this financial crisis".
The Conservative premier of Nova Scotia said they would be asking the federal government for a meeting and; "I want to emphasize not a meeting demanding more money". He said they may approach the Prime Minister to ensure that federal funding to the provinces is sufficient to maintain national standards in health care

and other social services. They "may" approach the Prime Minister to ensure that those standards are met.
The premiers of Atlantic Canada are not demanding that the federal government respond appropriately to the concerns of the people of Atlantic Canada. The three Liberal premiers and the one Conservative premier are basically saying; well, we have received a cut of over $100 million to the region but we are just going to say we do not like it, we are not going to stand up and fight against this Conservative government's cuts.
I think we can only say that it is shameful that those three Liberal premiers and that one Conservative premier are not fighting for the rights of the people of their region, are not fighting for the people who elected them, are not standing up for those people's opportunities in health care, education, employment and being able to stay in their own communities.
The government says it cannot do anything. It says that equalization payments are a formula and that the formula changes because of what goes on in the economy and that nothing basically can be done. It is just an accounting procedure that takes place and sometimes the numbers go up as a result of that accounting procedure and sometimes the numbers go down. Sometimes the provinces will get more money and sometimes less.
To the people who are affected by the loss of these millions of dollars it is a little bit different than that. It is about loss of opportunities, loss of employment and as we said before, loss of educational opportunities and loss of health care facilities.
The government forgets that when it says it cannot do anything in 1985 it did intervene to offset reductions in the 1985-1986 equalization payments to the provinces. It did provide supplements to the provinces of Atlantic Canada as a result of changes in the formula. If it did it then it can do it now. If it cared at all about the plight of people in Atlantic Canada, surely it would begin to address these concerns and make up the difference.
Another point regarding equalization payments which is worth making is that the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council has said-these are not just my words-that if Ontario had gone for a balanced budget rather than the modest deficit it introduced, then the situation in Atlantic Canada would have been much worse in terms of equalization payments. In other words, the Ontario deficit budget is something which has assisted Atlantic

Canada in making sure that the equalization payments did not reduce even further.
What that means is that Ontario is assisting to some considerable extent in the economic stabilization of the whole country while being attacked by the federal government and the Official Opposition and other provinces across this country.
While that attack is being directed towards Ontario it, in fact, as a result of its budgetary policies has assisted the less well off regions in Canada by ensuring that their equalization payments have not been reduced as much as they otherwise would.
We also have to ask why these equalization payments have reduced. Why do the have provinces have rather less to distribute in terms of equalization payments to those provinces who are less well off.
Again we have to look to the bankruptcy of federal government economic policies which clearly are not working across this country.
If I may say a few words about Saskatchewan, those same economic policies which the federal government pursues were pursued by the Conservative government in Saskatchewan until, thankfully, last Monday when they were turfed out of office by a party and a government that cares about creating jobs, cares about providing opportunities for people, cares about education and the health care system.
The very things that concern Atlantic Canadians, Saskatchewan people are concerned about as well. That is why they turfed out the government. That is why Mr. Devine and his Conservatives lost. They tried neo-conservative economic policies that simply do not work in the hinterland regions of Canada. Without a commitment from the government to make economic policy for people, those people in Atlantic Canada and those people in Saskatchewan will continue to be at a disadvantage.
We cannot allow these cuts to equalization payments to take place without criticism. We cannot allow Atlantic Canada to receive more than $100 million less than it otherwise would have received without voicing our strong opposition.
We in the New Democratic Party have called for the federal government to intervene to offset this reduction
in equalization transfer payments. We have called for more adequate Established Programs Financing transfers, instead of the federal government's contribution to health and post-secondary education reducing and reducing in percentage terms each year, so that rather than as they once paid 50 per cent of health care and post-secondary education costs in the provinces, it is now something a little over 35 per cent.
In other words, the federal government is not pulling its weight in ensuring that there is equal opportunity in those areas of health care and education across this country.
We could say a few words about the fishery and railways which are also mentioned in this resolution, but the clear point with regard to the fishery is that the strategies of this government and previous Liberal governments have been totally ineffective in ensuring the appropriate management of that fishery.
The reason we do not have enough fish for our fishermen and our fishing communities in Atlantic Canada is that the whole stock has been totally mismanaged and basically has been handed over to the interests of two large fishing corporations which really do not care about the regions they are working in but only care about making profits.
There are other ways to ensure that job opportunities can be created in these regions. We will see these other opportunities, other approaches as the New Democratic governments of Saskatchewan, British Columbia, Ontario and Yukon develop those policies as the Yukon and Ontario governments already are doing. We will see jobs created as a result of the resources within the communities rather than resorting to the only strategy that this government seems to understand, which is to resort to the marketplace, to private capital that is not interested in the creation of jobs in this economy in this country but is interested only in making profits.

provinces, thereby threatening the stability of the Atlantic provinces. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate with mixed emotions. I listened to a lot of speakers. A lot of numbers have been tossed around and a lot of reasons as to why things are getting better or why things are getting worse.
I listened to the Minister of Finance across the way, a man for whom I have an awful lot of respect. One of the phrases he uttered was that this talk is absolute nonsense. If this is the case, if this is absolute nonsense, I as him: Why is there a five-year freeze on the Established Programs Financing? Everybody had been talking about

this prior to the latest announcement the Atlantic premiers got.
Prince Edward Island would lose $12 million in transfer payments. Now the minister says that the transfer payments continue to rise. However, regarding the $12 million in the initial budget, it says here in a news report that Newfoundland in the new estimates is going to lose $110 million.
Will this not spell higher taxes? Will it not see fewer social programs? Most important, does this not sever the lifeline of Atlantic Canada? People spoke here this morning asking the Minister of Finance about the amount of money Atlantic Canada got compared to other provinces. I say to that member: yes, we would love to be a contributing province. I hope I live long enough to see the day when we are a contributing province. I believe the reason these transfer payments were put in place in the first place was to help these provinces and territories to maintain a standard of living equal to the rest of Canada.
As I see it unfolding, I believe the writing is clearly on the wall. I believe the fabric of social programs and medicare appears to be targeted as the first to go. As I said, smaller provinces and thinly populated territories will not be able to hold the system together or support the development of new or innovative specialty health programs.
How can the federal government expect small provinces to maintain national health standards when it freezes this EPF? In the past cash payments from the federal government have made it possible for Canadians to have highly developed systems of medicare and post-secondary education. Two weeks ago Premier Ghiz at the constitutional hearings in Charlottetown stated that one of his fears was that with these transfers of power to the provinces we would be a checker-board Canada with different levels of medical programs in different provinces across the country.
I believe that the health care gap can be measured by two standards: the have provinces and the have not provinces. We can translate this into terms of the people, which also translates into 10 to 11 years more longevity for the high income Canadians compared to that of low income Canadians. Moreover as our health care system advances we find people living longer lives. The cost of high-technology medical equipment is rising, but be-
Supply
cause of cuts in transfer payment, the provinces are forced either to slash essential services or to impose further taxes on an already overburdened taxpayer.
At one time Canada maintained national standards for health care and other basic services but no more. In the last budget the federal government vowed to maintain national standards through new legislation. Indeed we have a national standard: the slow death of medicare which has become the standard in every province.
In 1986 the present government finally recognized the health care gap. Let me quote what one of the Health and Welfare Canada's many documents said: "The first challenge we face is to find ways of reducing inequities in the health of low versus high income groups in Canada". Instead of doing this they introduced Bill C-69, the bill to limit funding to the provinces.
In his last budget, as in the one before it, the Minister of Finance continued to pass the buck to the provinces of this country. The federal government has simply transferred its federal fiscal problem to other levels of government. Smaller provinces will not be able to hold the system together or to support the development of new or innovative health programs. Moreover, the estimates of accumulative loss to provincial and territorial health care funding from 1986-1987 to 1994-1995 will total at least $22 billion.
It is frightening what this government is doing to what it once called a sacred trust of our community and country. With an aging population and the youth of my province having to relocate to central Canada to secure employment, P.E.I. has a higher than average age group. With this age group comes a greater demand for health care, and with a greater demand for health care of course comes a greater need for financing.
We saw what the freeze did in the federal-provincial transfer of payments in Newfoundland's last budget: 900 health care jobs and 360 hospital beds were lost due to cuts in the system. If this plan of action continues health care will be eliminated. The current medicare system, a source of national pride, respected and copied around the world will be but a dream.
In Prince Edward Island they now have to work harder and longer to achieve less than what is needed, at no fault of their own. In 1990 the average weekly earnings of industrial workers was the same as it was in 1975. What

Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Madam Speaker, a few weeks ago here in the House of Commons the Prime Minister unveiled his government's constitutional proposals, calling on Canadians to join him in shaping Canada's future together. In his remarks the Prime Minister said that his government's proposals have one simple but nevertheless critical and crucial objective: to build a stronger and more prosperous Canada where all Canadians can feel at home.
These are fine sentiments but they have a hollow ring in Atlantic Canada. For decades we have known the indignity of being the have not provinces, the poor cousins of Confederation. For generations the best and the brightest of our young people have all too often had to search for prosperity elsewhere because there was no opportunity for them to use their talents at home.
In recent years we have watched the slow and in some cases rapid decline of the pillars of our economy: ship building, the fishery and coal and steel in Cape Breton. We have had to accept unemployment insurance payments as a main component of our income and endure the condescension that has accompanied that dependence. Regional development has come to mean a code word for: we do not measure up.
The sense of being a have not region, of having to rely on Ottawa for regional assistance, has seeped into our consciousness in Atlantic Canada. It has reflected itself in our literature, in our music and even in our humour. It has eroded our pride. It has on occasion spilled out in violent confrontation, though we are not by nature violent.
The occupations of the fisheries officers in Port aux Basques recently or confrontations at the gates of the Sydney Steel plant are simply a manifestation of the frustrations we all face.
Last week I was in my constituency of Cape Breton Highlands- Canso where the official unemployment rate is in the order of 23 per cent. But everyone there knows that the percentage of the labour force out of work is much higher. Collie Herman Chisholm, the seasoned and generally optimistic mayor of Antigonish, told me when I asked him, because he remembers, that the job situation locally has never been this bad, not even during the great depression. He was calling me about the rail line from Truro to Sydney, which goes through Antigonish and which CN announced recently it was proposing to sell to a private bidder.
October 24, 1991

The main customer on this line is Stora Forest Industries, a pulp and paper mill located at Point Tupper on the Strait of Canso. It directly employs some 2,300 workers. The CN announcement came as Stora and its parent in Sweden, Stora Kopperberg, were considering modernization and expansion plans involving some $500 million to $600 million. Without some form of modernization in order to enable Stora to compete in the international pulp and newsprint market of the future, the president of Stora, Tom Hall, has suggested the mill would become non-competitive and die. That would spell catastrophe for the economy of eastern Nova Scotia and the thousands of families who depend in one way or another on this industry.
For Stora, guaranteed and reliable access to rail is absolutely vital. The uncertainty caused at this moment, even by CN's consideration of these plans which are objected to by everybody including the premier of Nova Scotia, could well be the factor that causes Stora's parent in Sweden to choose to invest elsewhere.
Yet, in the face of this CN persists and both ministers of transport refuse to intervene to stop this ludicrous move. No wonder the Prime Minister's invitation to participate in constitutional renewal has a hollow ring in Atlantic Canada.
A week or so ago I was in Baddeck where Judy MacDonald, a housewife and mother, took the time to write down her thoughts for me on the economic situation in Cape Breton in the wake of the Prime Minister's constitutional initiative.
I regret that time permits me to quote only a small portion of Judy's letter. She speaks for many in Cape Breton when she writes:
Much has been made of how hard central Canada has been hit by the recession. The joke around here is: "There is a recession. Someone should tell Cape Breton". The economy has gone from bad to worse. People in the depressed parts of Canada such as Cape Breton at this time cannot raise concerns about the Constitution or issues like it because they are trying to make ends meet and in extreme cases keep warm, fed and clothed. This is being interpreted as apathy toward our constitutional problems which is simply not the case. The only special status Cape Breton has is starvation.
Lately this House has devoted a fair deal of time and attention to the plight of the western farmer. Atlantic Canadians feel empathy for the western farmer. They

were inclined to be happy and supportive when at the urging of this party the government, admittedly on the eve of an election in Saskatchewan, came through with an $800 million package.
However, it is awfully hard for us not to feel shortchanged and betrayed when the fishermen in Newfoundland and Labrador, who this year faced a total collapse of their fishery, received a paltry $39 million in recycled money. The timing of this package was contrived to exclude other deserving fishermen in Atlantic Canada like the herring fishermen in the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence in Antigonish County who also faced a collapse of their catches and their income.
Then of course there is the government's refusal to assist the Scotia Synfuels project which has been under development for 10 years and which is tailor-made for the Cape Breton economy. The Synfuels project will create some 2,000 jobs. It will create a clean use for Cape Breton's most abundant resource, coal, and contribute to Canada's energy security. It is just as viable as Hibernia or OSLO or Syncrude or the Lloydminister upgrader project on the Saskatchewan and Alberta border into which the federal government has poured hundreds of millions of dollars.
Yet, on September 27, on the eve of the Saskatchewan election, the Lloydminister upgrader which straddles by coincidence the ridings represented by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture received an additional $175 million on top of nearly $300 million from a supposedly cash starved, deficit conscious federal government.
Nova Scotians are praying for a provincial election. They want an opportunity to throw out the incompetent, corrupt, Buchanan Tory government. They are starting to realize that perhaps if we have a provincial election we might get Ottawa to move and provide some of the assistance they have been denying us over the last several months. It seems that only provincial elections are what get this government moving.
This week the four provinces of Atlantic Canada received news that their entitlements under the equalization payments program for 1991 had fallen by some $140 million below what had been budgeted.

Yesterday and the day before, when we raised this matter during Question Period, all the Minister of Finance could do was to wave his arms helplessly and say that this was outside this control.
The equalization payments were determined by a formula, and the formula was written into legislation. The equalization payments are based on a formula, but what go into the formula are the tax bases of five of the provinces: Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba, British Columbia and Saskatchewan.
The size of these tax bases depends on the level and the growth of provincial income, in other words on the strength of the economy of places like Ontario. Everybody knows that this government's policies have created a recession which has crippled the Ontario manufacturing sector and flattened the Ontario economy so that the Ontario tax base, which is the principal generator of entitlements under the equalization formula has not been able to generate the entitlements.
Why did the government create this recession? It created this recession to squelch a bout of inflation which it created three years ago by abandoning its so-called commitment to the deficit, to deficit reduction, in order to buy the 1988 election.
It did this by jacking up real interest rates, pushing up the value of the Canadian dollar, choking off investment, stifling exports and killing jobs in Atlantic Canada as well as in Ontario. It did not matter that we in Atlantic Canada were not the source of the inflation. We had to swallow the medicine anyway so we got it both ways from this government.
Its economic policies have stifled our ability to generate wealth and jobs through exports and expansion, making us more dependent on equalization payments. Now, by crushing the economy that generates the source of these payments, the government denies them as well.
The Minister of Finance yesterday suggested that we on this side of the Flouse had a problem with the equalization payments formula. We have no problem with the equalization payments formula. The formula works. It is his economic policies that do not work.
It is time that this government stopped treating Atlantic Canadians like an appendage. It is time that this
government started realizing that we are part of this country and, if the government wants us to be a part of constitutional renewal, it has to treat our economies as just as important as those economies of the rest of this country.

I am from central Ontario and I do not begrudge one bit of that. I wish in our province we could have 42, 46 or 47 per cent of our budget coming from the federal government. We do not. We have because of our geographical location a lot of advantages that the out-reaches of this country do not have. We are prepared to pay our fair share and are doing that.
For the hon. member to stand and say that this government does not care or have concern for the eastern part of this country is not fair. As a matter of fact we have put together ACOA, a program exclusively for

the eastern part of this country to diversify the economy, to encourage growth there. None of these organizations are ever funded enough because they always want more and more and more. Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the minister for his comments. I would like to correct some of the impressions which he received from my speech a minute ago.
The point of the argument and the point that people in Atlantic Canada are trying to make to this government is not that our underlying aim is to get more equalization payments. It is that we are seeking to strengthen our economy so that we will not have to depend on equalization payments.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak today about this subject because I am also one of those who is working day in and day out to strengthen the Atlantic economy and to strengthen it on a long-term basis.
I must say that the previous speaker, the hon. member from Cape Breton, has not been really straight with this House or straight with his constituents when he blames the economic circumstances of Canada today on the policies of this government.
He makes no reference at all to the 20 years or more of deficit spending that his predecessor government conducted in this country. It left us with a burden of debt that we have not been able to service without incurring continuing deficits.
Only through the budget recoveiy plan introduced by the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre when he was Minister of Finance and now being carried on by the hon. Deputy Prime Minister do we have any prospect of ultimately eradicating that deficit, balancing our budget and commencing to pay down the tremendous debt with

Supply
which we have been left as a heritage of more than two decades of Liberal governments.
For the hon. member from Cape Breton to gloss over that fact is to mislead his constituents and to mislead the entire Atlantic region in their perception of the economic circumstances which we face.
The situation in which we find ourselves today and the motion by the hon. member for Gander-Grand Falls are based on an October calculation of equalization payments that unfortunately has resulted in shortfalls from expectations in the equalization revenues of three of the provinces in the Atlantic region. The worst of those has occurred in my own province of New Brunswick where it appears that the expectation will be short in excess of $100 million, amounting to about 2.61 per cent of the annual entitlement of $4.2 billion.
I think it is important to put our mind around that subject. The equalization entitlement to New Brunswick is $4.2 billion. On this occasion it appears that the follow-up data that reinforce the estimates on which these formulas are built indicate that the expectation in the estimates were too high and the past payments were too high. This adjustment occurs as a result of a formula that has been enshrined in legislation for many years, long before this government took office. It continues to be enshrined with the same formula that pertains today as it did then. That formula has on this occasion sadly resulted in a shortfall of expectations.
I sympathize with the ministers of finance in those provinces who have to experience that shortfall, who have to confront the reality that their budgets are going to be seen to be too ambitious, too optimistic, and who are going to have to adjust them downward.
It has not always been a shortfall situation. Regarding New Brunswick, I have a clipping from the Saint John Telegraph Journal of July 5, 1990 in which the hon. minister of finance for the province of New Brunswick advised that he was experiencing great exaltation as a result of a windfall of $47 million, a surplus beyond expectations. His estimates were too conservative and the realities of the transfer from the federal government were to be $47 million higher than he expected. This process of formula financing works out over time to
produce the truth that the equalization formula is intended to reveal.
I would like to read into the record a few other facts. I am going to address particularly the New Brunswick circumstances this morning because New Brunswick had by far the greatest hit in terms of the decrease of budget expectations as a result of this October adjustment calculation of the equalization payment.
Major federal transfers to New Brunswick will total an increase of about 4.4 per cent over 1991-92. Per capita, New Brunswick will receive over $2,200 per person in 1992-93 which is almost 75 per cent higher than the national average. That is a statistic which demonstrates that the equalization concept is working.
The budget change in EPF transfers which I will address later on will account for only two-tenths of one per cent of provincial revenues in 1992. It is a negligible decrease. Again it is a decrease in expectation, not a decrease in dollars.
The major federal transfers will continue to account for a very high percentage of New Brunswick's total revenue. More than 39 per cent of New Brunswick's 1992-93 budget will come from federal transfers.
I would say that the only slashing and burning, as somebody has characterized the adjustment calculations, taking place is the abuse of fact. As the minister emphasized earlier this morning-and I am glad to repeat it-federal transfers to the provinces are not being cut. The Atlantic provinces are not being singled out. Health care and education are not being placed at risk.
I would just like to say that with respect to Established Programs Financing, the foundation for federal transfers to education and health, the total dollars to New Brunswick were $543 million in 1989-90. They were $546 million in 1990-91, and they will be over $550 million this year. They will grow in actual dollars again next year.
It is an abuse of fact when people say that EPF funding has been cut. The rate of growth of EPF funding has been cut and there are good reasons for that, which I will also get to in a moment. What is really happening is that our federal government is continuing to implement and build on the agenda for economic recovery which we introduced last February.
October 24, 1991

It is a plan for a strong, solid recovery that is already helping to put the recession behind us and set the foundations for continuing non-inflationary growth. It is a plan that asks Canadians, including other levels of government, to work more effectively in a partnership for prosperity.
Not surprisingly the budget had important implications for federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, particularly for parts of the system and major transfers to provinces which consist of equalization, Established Programs Financing and the Canada Assistance Plan. These programs account for more than 90 per cent of all funding from the federal government to the provinces to help pay for a variety of very important services right across Canada.
For decades the federal government has provided large and growing financial support to the provinces in these respects. This year alone total federal transfers including both cash and tax transfers will reach almost $37 billion. Just the cash portion of the transfers accounts for one-fifth of all federal program spending.
Again let me echo the words of the minister. These transfers are simply too large to exempt from our expenditure restraint program. The deficit is a national problem and it demands a national solution. More important, it should be understood that in slowing the growth of transfer payments the federal government is seeking to encourage all levels of government to live realistically within their means, just as the federal government itself is called upon to do with its own programs.
It is significant to understand that for the past seven years the federal level of spending has grown at the rate of 3.7 per cent, versus a provincial average of 7.2 per cent. It just makes common sense that the federal government, in its responsibility on behalf of all Canadians, has to ask the other levels of government which constitute such a large part of its total expenditure program to restrain their spending within limits that are imposed upon the federal government itself.
The measures announced in the 1990 budget included a per capita freeze on EPF transfers. Although EPF transfers in total will continue to grow, as I have said in the New Brunswick case, with the population of each province, they will be frozen until 1994-95 at present
Supply
rates of growth. There will continue to be no limit on Canada Assistance Plan contributions to less wealthy provinces. In addition, equalization transfers to the less wealthy provinces have been totally exempted from the budget expenditure controls.
For this motion to suggest that the levels of equalization transfers have been reduced is, as the hon. minister said earlier, simply not so.
The measures we have taken bring the growth of federal-provincial transfers into line with the current fiscal realities. In fact the rate of transfers will be at 3.7 per cent, whereas the rate of federal spending in all other areas will be at 3.4 per cent.
I am convinced that most Canadians know that the deficit and the debt are serious problems that must be solved. They know that firm determined action is needed to solve these problems. They believe this should be carried out with the least possible adverse impact on those in the greatest need. That is the way that the equalization formula and the application of the changes to the EPF funding and to the CAP funding have all been designed.
In the 1989 budget the government set out a medium term fiscal plan to reduce the deficit sharply and to bring an end to new government borrowing in financial markets by 1994-1995. That will be a welcome day. The 1990 budget reaffirmed this plan and introduced a program of expenditure control to meet it.
However, because the recession revenues are now lower than forecast, expenditures are higher due to the weak economy. We have an even more difficult road as we work toward that very enviable prospect of a balanced budget some day.
The motion which is before us refuses to recognize the importance of deficit reduction and debt control. It implies that we should not only be spending more than ever but that we should be making no effort to set reasonable limits on future spending growth. Of course that is hardly surprising. Both parties of the opposition have impeccable credentials when it comes to living the philosophy of credit card finance: spend now, borrow more tomorrow, and worry about the consequences next year or next decade. It is easy to contemplate and talk

October 24, 1991
Supply
only about sharing the wealth when one does not take any responsibility for creating it.
The problem is that next year or next decade is now. We have seen how living beyond our country's means, including provincial transfers that increase at a rate well above inflation, can lead to a growing burden of public debt. In 1984 when this government took office the federal government was handing out $1.33 in programs and services for every $1 it collected in taxes. Mr. Speaker, how long could you live on your budget if you were spending $1.33 on services for every $1 you were earning? That was no bargain then and it is no bargain now. In fact we are now paying the price over and over again for too many years of consuming more government service than we were willing to pay for.
This fiscal year our public debt is forecast to reach $419 billion. That is more than $15,000 for every man, woman and child in Canada. The interest rate alone on the debt will eat up more than $43 billion this year, more than we spend on old age security, unemployment insurance and family allowances combined.
In the 1991 budget the government has asked Canadians to share the burden of further financial restraint. We recognize the sacrifices that many Canadians have already made in the name of restraint and we know there will be some reluctance to accept the necessity for more of the same.
If we took no steps to deal with this worsening fiscal situation, the deficit would be much higher than the forecast by many billions of dollars. This would aggravate all of the fundamental problems which must be solved if we are to ensure a strong recovery and a return to prosperity in the years ahead. Further increased spending would only make the debt problem that much worse.
In the 1991 budget the government has taken the tough responsible decisions necessary to ensure Canada's finances become healthy again. As a result of measures announced in that budget the government will hold the deficit to $30.5 billion this year. Despite the pressures of the recession the deficit will fall in 1992-1993 to $25 billion below that level for the first time in more than a decade. Growth in program spending will be held to an average of no more than 3 per cent in the years after 1991-1992 on an annual basis and the need for new federal borrowing in financial markets will
be eliminated after 1993-1994. The 1991 budget includes measures providing Canadians with added assurances that these targets will be met.
In a significant change that alters the way that government manages expenditures we have released draft legislation which will impose mandatory limits on annual program spending for the next five years. That is the first time in history that the Government of Canada has legislated in law its spending restraints and budget limitations. We have tabled legislation to set up the debt servicing and reduction fund and have committed that all revenues from the goods and services tax and from privatization will go to the servicing of the deficit and the reduction of the debt. These revenues will be applied first against the servicing of the debt and, as they grow over time, will be used to reduce the outstanding debt.
The effort to reduce spending and the deficit will be reinforced by these government decisions to set its targets clearly in law. Through the plan for economic recovery the federal government will take action to establish fiscal stability and to strengthen confidence in Canada's future.
I know my time is running short, but I want to make a very important illustration of the importance of federal transfers to Atlantic Canada. In Atlantic Canada the total of all forms of federal spending and financial contribution in 1988 was $8.2 billion more than the contribution of revenues from Atlantic Canada to the federal Treasury. These figures are three years old and are in fact higher today. That represents $3,600 per person in Atlantic Canada. As I say, that is a higher figure today. In 1988 those figures in Newfoundland were $2.4 billion; in Prince Edward Island it was $600,000 per year; $3 billion in Nova Scotia; and $2.2 billion in New Brunswick.
It is clear in the context of this debate that the federal government is not diminishing its commitment to Atlantic Canada. These figures speak extremely strongly for the Atlantic commitment to a strong Canadian entity, a prospering, and lasting Canadian unification.
I do not think anything could speak in fiscal terms more abundantly and more clearly than do these numbers. The impact of them is not well understood by Atlantic Canadians. It is a subject that as we contemplate our place in Canada we have to confront realistically and
October 24, 1991

not with the misleading implications of this motion or those on the other side who have spoken to it.
The adjustments that we have seen today in the equalization formula do not represent a threat to the welfare of Atlantic Canada. This is not a special burden being placed on the maritimes or on Newfoundland. It is a reflection of a continuing equalization program that is strong, lasting and valuable. It is a continuing commitment to share the benefits of Canada among all of its citizens.
It is also important that we share the challenge of getting our punishing national debt under control. It also addresses that. Exempting provinces from this challenge of debt reduction would be indeed to treat them as second-class citizens. The ultimate result would be to put Canada in jeopardy of becoming a second-class country.
Just as I finish, I should say as well that the entire system of federal-provincial transfers may well need adjustment. Perhaps it is time. I understand the Minister of Finance has sent some signals that in 1992 and subsequently those formulas may be reviewed and readjusted. For example, the regular recalculations under the equalization plan obviously do pose problems for provincial budgetary planning and program management.
I can sympathize with the ministers of finance in those provinces who today have to adjust their prospects. As stated in the February budget, the system of transfers to the provinces including equalization will be reviewed with a view to examining reforms that may be necessary.
Recommendations from the Atlantic provinces' premiers and their ministers of finance, such as those from their meetings yesterday and today, will be very helpful. They will help this federal government to reinforce Canadian Confederation as a fiscally sound and responsible agency, able not only to defend the financial sovereignty of this country but to share the dividends of prosperity in this country with all who participate in this Confederation, including the Atlantic region.

SIDS, which is sometimes referred to as crib death, strikes down apparently healthy babies suddenly and unexpectedly, leaving behind grieving families and a powerless medical profession.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague from Kingston and the Islands.

That is a very good question that my hon. colleague has asked. The answer is quite simple. There is a rate at which Established Programs Financing is given to the provinces that receive it. The rate accelerates each year under a certain formula. This government has decided to freeze the rate. So while there is a dollar increase, there is an over-all cut because of all of the costs increasing.
For example, I did not even get close to discussing some of the problems faced by universities relating to the GST on a lot of purchasing they have to make, particularly in the area of library books and things of this nature. The fact that the rate is frozen, and is frozen until 1994-95, means that they are not keeping ahead of the game.
A very good example with regard to universities is the question of books.
When I was a first year law student at Dalhousie University in 1971, and the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands will remember this because he was there just a year before that- Yes, we were both very young going to law school.
The member will remember that there is a torts textbook that is used by all first year law students, called Wright and Linden, standard in all common law schools in the country. I was fortunate, I bought my text from my aunt who actually was a classmate of the member for Kingston and the Islands. I did not buy it, she gave it to me. Families are like that.

speechtext: I did not know he was that old.

However, to get the point here, my textbook was given to me so I was very lucky. I was lucky that I had a member of my family who had been there just before me. The cost of that textbook in 1971, brand new, was somewhere in the vicinity of $20 to $22. It is an absolute. You must have it. Also, the editions change as the law changes. Stephen Leacock said years ago when writing about a Canadian university that all you needed for a university was a few people, a few chairs and a few books. Well, we have progressed passed that in the sense of the way our universities work today. Mr. Leacock was rightly talking in a sense of the philosophy of education.
We in this country know that education is more than philosophy, it is training. Even if it is only a few books, as Mr. Leacock suggested, we are taking away the money from the universities for those books.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that others have said the same thing, but it is not really a pleasure to rise and debate this particular issue because of the hardship that has been caused to Atlantic Canadians as a result of the government's high-handed practice in the area of transfer payments.
This is just one aspect of a continuing story of how the government is setting up an arrangement where it is going to have a patchwork Confederation. The equality which was enshrined in our Constitution is going to be lost because the government does not have either the financial desire, wherewithal or whatever reason to make sure that there is equality. It may have the wherewithal, but it does not really have the total desire to hold this country together and have the proper sharing between the rich and the poor.
In New Brunswick, we are going to lose about $110 million in transfer payments. Our province will have to find that $110 million somewhere or cut back on service as the alternative. That, quite frankly, is unacceptable because those areas that are going to be adversely affected are obviously the areas of education and health care in particular. Those two areas are the ones that should be least affected by any change in transfer payments.

When we look at this problem, it is hard not to be a little embarrassed, coming from Atlantic Canada and sounding like the poor cousin who is always asking for a handout or the dole so to speak. I find it kind of reprehensible that I have to stand up here and say that there should be equalization among provinces and that Atlantic Canadians are hard done by and therefore need more money. That is the reality of the situation.
If we are going to provide proper medicare and proper educational services, if we are going to provide the basic needs of Canadians including Atlantic Canadians, then transfer payments are necessary and this is what we are going to need.
This formula does not work because those Atlantic Canada provinces that are pulling themselves up by their bootstraps are starting to accomplish something, are finding themselves penalized by their success. New Brunswick has been doing reasonably well in these tough economic times. Through the good leadership of a Liberal government in New Brunswick, success is being achieved to a degree.
It is now going to be penalized by that success. Because it is doing so well, it is going to have a larger cut than any other Atlantic province. I believe the numbers are around $110 million for New Brunswick and about $17 million for P.E.I. and $18 million for Newfoundland, or something like that. Nova Scotia is going to get a little increase.
The province that is going to bear the brunt is quite frankly and quite candidly the province which has had the most success. That is another inequity in this situation. What you are doing is taking that success and eventually turning it into failure.
If these moneys were invested properly, which is what New Brunswick has done in the past, then we would see an improved educational system, an improved higher educational system. You would see a health care system that responds to the needs, an efficient health care system.
Instead, what we are going to have to see are cuts and more cuts. This will have the effect of taking something away from the system rather than making it work.
I would like to quote from Premier McKenna who is now talking quite justifiably about a new transfer formula because this One obviously is not working. "The
formula reduces transfers to provinces whose economies are improving. When that combines with the recession hitting Canada's wealthiest province, the result is a massive reduction in payments."
"What we have seen this year should never be repeated. We are a victim of New Brunswick's economic success and Ontario's economic failure. The combined effect has given us an absolutely shocking decrease in equalization. The current system is flawed by being attached to the economy of Ontario."
"When Ontario's economy does as well as it was until the recession struck early last year, the rest of the country follows on its coat tails. When Ontario's economy falters and the have not provinces need assistance, the formula should reward them. But it doesn't. The system is also designed to help provinces whose economies are floundering, but in doing so punishes those governments who tiy to improve their situation". McKenna said he wants to see a new formula negotiated, possibly as a part of future constitutional talks which would encourage poorer provinces to prudently manage their money, keeping deficits low and encourage investment.
I think that is the nub of the point. What happens is that the provinces who have not been successful, the provinces who have not managed their finances properly, are rewarded in these circumstances and the provinces who have done a good job, who have kept an even keel, have bit bullet, so to speak and gone through the trauma of wage freezes, cutbacks and reorganizations in trying to accord a proper balance in the system and at the same time trying to encourage economic development, are penalized.
I think the premier is right when he says that we are going to have to look at this from a constitutional basis. As I read our Constitution as it presently exists there appears to be a constitutional requirement of equality. By this formula that equality is lost. All you have to do is visit any of the hospitals in Atlantic Canada, talk to the people who are managing those hospitals and realize the sheer impact of what is going on.
In my own community of Moncton, we have wards in the hospital that have to be closed, so they are not there to provide the necessary health care service. We have elective surgery being deferred for six, eight and nine
October 24, 1991

months because we do not have the resources to provide the service in the area of health care.
That is a very serious problem for our province. That is why there is a national responsibility to assist New Brunswick and to encourage it. If New Brunswick is given that type of encouragement and that financial support, one day we will be contributing to Ontario's poor economy and we will have transfers coming from New Brunswick to Ontario. That is what we are aiming to do so that we in turn, as we helped out the west during the depression in the thirties, will be able to help Ontario through its tough economic times. We can do that by making New Brunswick and Atlantic Canada strong.
This does just the opposite. This puts Atlantic Canada further behind. It is going to be less able to be a full partner in this Confederation. That is why we have an obligation in this House to see that that does not happen. That is why we need this government to recognize that the formula is wrong, that the formula does not work, it penalizes success and it rewards those who are unsuccessful, all of which in my view, and I am sure in the view of many members opposite, is simply wrong.
As we proceed through this debate and look at what is going on in our country and as we talk about a new federation or confederation, I think that this is going to have to be one aspect discussed, that we try to find a different formula, a different system. We have to do something in the area of education because that is going to be the one main vehicle that is going to allow Atlantic Canadians to be full partners in this Confederation, that is going to be the saviour in my view of all of Atlantic Canadians. It is going to allow Atlantic Canadians to stay in Atlantic Canada rather than having to emigrate to Ontario, Quebec or out west because there are not the jobs and not the fulfilment that one would expect.
I know that my time is running short, Mr. Speaker. Let me say this. It is not a proud moment to be standing here cap in hand saying we need to receive some money from those who are richer and who are better off than we are. The reality is that this is an investment, not an expenditure. It is an investment in Atlantic Canadians. In the long run, it will pay a dividend to all of Canada.
