speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this afternoon to take part in this debate which implies that the federal government is doing something to the Atlantic provinces that it does not do to anyone else, that threatens the stability of health care and education and that condemns the government for its destructive policy toward the fishery, the railway and the post office.
This afternoon we heard in Question Period questions put from the Atlantic province members concerning various government programs, that the provincial premiers and their own governments could do abetter job of it administering these things.
I would like to put on the record this afternoon that the Government of Canada currently has 50 federal-provincial agreements in effect in Atlantic Canada. These agreements cover a wide range of initiatives from highways to high-tech projects.
With the exception of one initiative for youth forestry in Newfoundland, all these agreements are already jointly managed with the provinces and the vast majority are implemented by provincial governments.
These federal-provincial agreements have been signed under the umbrella of economic and regional development agreements with each province in 1984. These ERDAs establish joint priorities for each of the provinces and provide a process for changing priorities as economic circumstances warrant. ERDA priorities have changed since 1984, and these have been revised accordingly to reflect emerging issues.
As to ACOA funds currently being directed to the private sector through its action program, these funds are intended to promote job creation, increased earned income, entrepreneurship, innovation and technology development, and increased trade among others. Surely the provinces cannot disagree with these federal priorities.
I would like to take the next few minutes to discuss various things that are taking place within the fisheries. The Government of Canada is following a strong integrated set of policies to achieve important goals for the Canadian fisheries: first, a strong Atlantic fishing industry in a more diversified and self-reliant economy; second, a stable Pacific fishery dealing successfully with allocation issues at home and capable of competing in a strenuous international environment; third, an environment against destructive foreign overfishing; fourth, protection of the aquatic environment; fifth, an aboriginal fisheries policy recognizing the important rights of native peoples in Canada's fisheries and encouraging their participation in the management of these resources; sixth, an increased development of recreational fisheries; seventh, promotion of ocean based industries and development; and finally a review of fisheries management structures and institutional mechanisms.
We are making important progress on all of these fronts. Our challenge in Atlantic Canada is both short term and long term. Fishermen in many parts of Atlantic Canada this year faced the worst environmental conditions in memory. The Government of Canada has responded quickly and comprehensively to this crisis, beginning in May with payments totalling $18 million as compensation for severe ice conditions which delayed or prevented thousands of fishermen from pursuing their livelihood. More recently, with the inshore season largely over and the extent of catch failure assessed, this government announced further assistance of $39 million in a program of employment measures, fish processing opportunities and gear-up payments for more than
10,000	fishermen and plant workers in Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and the Quebec lower north shore.
This assistance totalling more than $57 million is targeted to help meet critical needs across the Atlantic provinces. The employment measures alone are creating more than 45,000 weeks of work, much of it contributing directly to essential work on small craft harbours, fish habitat and the maintenance of fish plants.
October 24, 1991

Catch failure is a recurring problem. Part of our long-term strategy is to find permanent structures or approaches to the income and employment problems that fishermen and plant workers in one area or another face every year.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, along with the Minister of Employment and Immigration, will be consulting with the provinces, the fishing industry and unions to address these problems.
I might add that we do not have all the answers ourselves, but we look to others who are in the industry. We also look to the provinces to assist us in developing these programs.
Foreign overfishing is a serious problem. At recent meetings of the northwest Atlantic fisheries organizations we were able to make some progress against overfishing outside Canada's 200-mile limit by countries of the European community.
A new control system has been adopted called the hail system, to try to ensure vessels keep to their quotas. We continue to press for more comprehensive improvements to the international control measures outside the 200-miles. European ministers realize the situation is serious. There is a great deal of misinformation, some of it intentional, about foreign fishing inside the Canadian zone. We only allow into the zone fleets from countries that co-operate with us in conservation outside the 200-mile zone.
Those allowed into the zone to fish are only allowed to take fish that Canadians do not want to catch. If the foreigners did not catch these fish no one else would and they would go to waste.
Every foreign vessel carries a Canadian observer at the vessel's expense, and these vessels are policed rigidly to see they fish only what we allow them to fish.
These vessels provide benefits to Canadians. Their operators buy fish from Canadians. They land fish at Canadian plants providing employment for Canadians. They transfer their technology to Canadians and they also do research that we need in our waters.
A limited and controlled foreign fishery in Canadian waters is not an evil. It brings benefits that Canadians should appreciate, and many do. The government is committed to ending foreign overfishing outside the 200
Supply
miles by the present process if possible and by whatever means needed consistent with international law.
In the Pacific area important progress is being made toward international agreements to end driftnet fishing. Canada is in the forefront of international efforts to stop driftnet fishing and to promote high seas fishery conservation. Current developments include a new Ca-nada-U.S.-Japan-U.S.S.R. convention which is expected to stop high seas salmon fishing in the north Pacific in the summer of 1992 and a new UN resolution to stop all driftnet fishing in the North Pacific this summer as well.
Mr. Speaker, you will recall when we were in Japan last week that we raised this question of driftnet fishing. You were there and heard the discussion that took place with the Japanese on this very critical problem that we face.
We are strengthening the management of fisheries in this country. Members opposite supported the government last year in amending the Fisheries Act. The changes strengthened our conservation strategy and the long-term rebuilding of stocks by providing increased penalties for illegal fishing and damage to fish habitat. We are now entering the second year of the Atlantic Fisheries Adjustment Program which is devoting $584 million to rebuilding fish stocks, adjustments for individuals and communities, and opportunities for diversification.
Through AFAP our scientific research programs have been expanded by $40 million. We are increasing our knowledge base to rebuild stocks of northern cod, northern gulf cod, Scotia groundfish and snow crab. We are implementing new conservation measures to protect young fish and expanding surveillance and enforcement. We are working with the provinces to support older plant workers and trawlermen seeking opportunities outside the fishery.
Economic diversification projects are directing significant funding to underutilized species, fisheries development, aquaculture and marketing.
Court decisions of late, notably the decision in Sparrow, are not only clarifying aboriginal fisheries rights but spelling out an important duty for the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to protect and support those rights. DFO faces a great challenge to work with native

October 24, 1991
Supply
people and others in the fishery to sustain and build fish stocks while providing for native participation. Native participation will take many forms, not the least of which is co-management of stock enhancement, fish habitat programs and opportunities in both the commercial and recreational sectors.
On the Pacific coast and in Atlantic Canada DFO is playing a vital leadership role to resolve these complex issues through consensus and co-operation with native and other interests, as well as the local governments themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the speech that my colleague has just given. He has touched on one aspect of the Atlantic economy, the fisheries, which has been in a state of mismanagement and decline since this government took power.
I can take a great deal of exception to his comments as to whether the fisheries aid package which has been recently announced is timely, because it is not and whether it is adequate, because it is not.
Contrary to the statements that the member made, I want to make sure that the public is not intentionally or unintentionally misled into believing that all the fishermen in the Burin Peninsula in Newfoundland down to Cape Breton are jumping up and down with glee saying: "Thank you, thank you, thank you federal Tory government", because they are not.
What this government has clearly done has been too little too late. It has caused the collapse in the fishery by allowing too much foreign overfishing, and it has not provided the funds for diversification both of the fishery and of product market overseas.
That is not what I am going to speak on. I want to ask the member who has given his two cents worth on fish, although it is absolutely entirely wrong, does he believe in the principle of equalization? It is a principle that this country has been built on.
I mentioned this earlier, in our Constitution Act, 1982 is enshrined the principle of equalization. It says that one of the underpinnings of this country is that funds shall be transferred into areas to ensure that national standards
and programs will be available to all, no matter where they live.
Does he not agree that in an area of less than 2.4 million people the cutbacks since 1988 in excess of $1.5 billion in regional development grants, the cutbacks of hundreds of millions of dollars in transfers through EPF for health care and the cutback of hundreds of millions of dollars in EPF to post-secondary education coupled with the recent cut of $170 million will ensure that those provinces on the Atlantic coast, the four Atlantic provinces which had a very limited tax base, do not have the flexibility to recapture through additional taxation the moneys that are lost?
Does he not believe that this is eroding the principle of equalization and the ability of those provinces to deliver services of national standards to the people who live in the Atlantic?

speechtext:
The quick answer is no. The reason I say that is because I believe in equalization payments.
A formula has been developed. A formula has been enshrined in law. This year it just so happens that the total economy of Canada is down.

If a government could turn on the economy by the snap of its fingers, would we not be very stupid not to? If we have so much influence over the economy, would we not be foolish on this side not to turn on the tap and make sure the economy is robust?
The way you are sounding is that we are deliberately trying to turn things down. Nothing could be further from the truth. They are talking about us singling out Atlantic Canada here. There is a deficit in this country. Have you ever once mentioned the deficit? Get your head out of the sand. We have a horrendous deficit in this country and unless we come to grips with it we are going to go down the tubes.
There is a sharing that has to take place across this country. There has not been one cut made to any program to Atlantic Canada that has not been made to every other province in the country.
That is simply not true.

That is true, and you know it.

I would like you to clarify that.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George -Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to join in the debate on a very important motion that I think is correct in all its wording condemning the current government for reducing the level of transfer payments to the Atlantic provinces, thereby threatening the stability of health care and education" and further condemning "the government for its destructive policies toward the fishery, the railway and the post office". It is really treating the different regions of Canada in a very unfair way. The policies of this government are shown to have failed. It has pursued neo-conservative economic policies, the Thatcher and Reagan agenda that is being thrown out of the window by voters across Canada. We hope that will happen soon in a federal election in the next year or two when Canadians have an opportunity to judge this government on its economic policies.
What I would like to do in the time that I have is just talk briefly a bit about the question of equalization payments, the reductions that are taking place there, the
fishery concerns in the Atlantic provinces, and a bit about forestry matters which unfortunately were not covered in the Liberal motion. I then would like to mention what we think are a couple of proposals that the people in Atlantic Canada would approve of. We hope they are listening to this debate today, hearing the debate and making some observations about what members in this House have to say about the concerns and the mess that this government has got us into.
The members of the government side say that there is no money, that the deficit is rising and that we have to be concerned about that. That is true. Just recently this government extended a $1 billion line of credit to Saddam Hussein. If Saddam Hussein moved to Halifax this government might then be prepared to help out the Atlantic provinces more than it is now.
All we have to look at is how many millions of dollars are going to be cut to the Atlantic provinces because of the activities of this government. According to news reports, primarily from the premiers' conference held recently, Newfoundland will be losing $20 million, Nova Scotia will lose $21 million, Prince Edward Island will lose $11 million, and New Brunswick will lose $64 million. The total-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I just wonder if I could correct an extremely serious error which the hon. member has made about the $1 billion line of credit. It is not to Iraq. It was to Iran. It is not the government of Saddam Hussein. I think that should be corrected for the record.

Again it points out that the government is more prepared to help countries outside Canada than it is its own regions in Canada. It is important that Canadians understand that. Those lines of credit and funds could go to help many parts of this country.

What do we have in the maritimes? We have a Tory premier so far. We do not know how long he will be in office, and then we have three Liberal premiers. They are really tough. They are going to meet with the federal government. I think these premiers out there are wimp-
October 24, 1991

ing out on their own provinces and on representing the interests of the people there.
It has come to the point where it is not just going to be the elected people in this House speaking out and trying to defend Atlantic Canada. It is going to be the people of the maritimes and Newfoundland and Labrador, who will be speaking out. As one member already mentioned, they are phoning the offices of members of Parliament saying how ridiculous this government's policies are and that it should be thrown out of office at the earliest opportunity.
Let us take a look at some of the resource issues, critical issues not just to the maritimes and Newfoundland and Labrador but to all parts of Canada and the management of those resources. We have had a lot of debate in this House about the concerns over the fishery in the maritimes. There has not been as much debate, unfortunately, over concerns about forestry in the maritimes.
Let us take a look at what some people have said about the fishery issue in Atlantic Canada. Perhaps it is dragging out the debate to point fingers at Liberals and Conservatives, but at some point I think it is important that people understand which governments were in office while this was happening.
As some background to just how important the fishery is to the people in Atlantic Canada, just let me quote from the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council: "The fishery is arguably the most important single industry in Atlantic Canada. Over 100,000 people are directly employed in harvesting and processing in more than 1,300 communities. Over half of these towns and villages depend solely on fishing".
It is clear that in the whole debate around management of our fisheries resource, the whole question of foreign overfishing, is an issue that has been mishandled by this government and previous governments.
Let us take a quick look at the record. In April 1989 the Prime Minister committed the federal government to putting an end to the practice of foreign overfishing, and nothing has been done.
At the November 1989 First Ministers' Conference, the Prime Minister was told that between 1986 and 1989 the European community had overfished the Grand Bank by some 600 per cent over the quota set by NAFO. Nothing was done.
Supply
In February of this year a press release from the Department of External Affairs indicated that the European community had taken five times more fish in 1990 than it was allocated. It is incredible what this country is allowing to happen to the most important resource for the maritimes. It seems that the government has washed its hands of the entire matter, thus putting into question the survival of many of the communities that depend on the fishing industry for their very survival, whether they will continue to exist.
One of the comments made in some of the reports on the fundamental problems with the infrastructure in the maritimes is that along with the high unemployment and the fewer jobs being created people are leaving the area. Nothing can be worse for an area than when the young people leave and move to major centres. More problems are created in the major urban centres that we cannot handle. We have to give reasons and opportunities for people to want to stay in the fishing and forestry communities because that is where their livelihoods are.
That is where we hope young people will return and stay to help develop and improve the life of people there. In our party we have said that Canada should move toward extending control over the entire Grand Bank including the nose and tail. The organization charged with protecting it, NAFO, has failed to do so. We have to provide more and more effort in this area to ensure that Canada's fishery resource is not overfished as has happened in most cases to date under this government.
As I mentioned earlier, one particular concern that is not mentioned in the motion is the issue of forestry. I have two general comments I would like to make in that regard.
To the best of my knowledge-and I stand to be corrected on this-we have yet to ensure that the forest agreement between the federal and provincial governments is signed in Nova Scotia. If some members opposite can tell me otherwise I hope they will. That is an important agreement and, if done properly, it will ensure that both levels of government co-operate in the management of our forests.
We even signed an agreement in British Columbia under the former Social Credit government. It did not come anywhere near what was needed, but with all the

difficulties that provincial government had we managed to sign an agreement. Now, for some reason, there seems to be an inability by the federal government here and the provincial government in Nova Scotia actually to sign that agreement. Maybe we are waiting for an election. I do not know. That could be the case. I guess we will have to wait until that election is called and then likely we will find out how quickly the announcement can be made.
I have had the opportunity to visit a number of the Atlantic provinces and, this past summer, to have paid a visit to a number of the forestry operations there. I found it very interesting. Of course many of the concerns and problems of the people in Nova Scotia are similar to those in my part of the country in British Columbia. It is an example of the problems in the forest industry. This government has followed a laissez-faire or a hands off the economy approach, unless of course one is a friend of the Conservatives. Then it is socialism all the way, but for anybody else, average Canadians, it is free enterprise: let the market do whatever it wants. Resulting from that many in the maritimes have alleged a rip-off of our fisheries and forestry resources.
What do we do when mills and what have you are run down? It takes millions of dollars of new capital to invest and rebuild. We end up with people who are thrown on the trash heap because they are not needed any more.
One of the major problems of course in the Nova Scotia area is the older mills. Some have alleged that the high dollar pursued by this government is a hidden part of the free trade agreement with the United States. That is certainly hurting the Nova Scotia area and economy. During the earlier debate members mentioned ACOA as one of the proposals that this government has put together. We have a western diversification office in western Canada and ACOA in Nova Scotia. I also hope we take a look at one of the criticisms I heard of ACOA when I was in the area which is that it seemed to be reluctant to encourage local development and local ideas. It seemed to be more excited about ideas coming in from elsewhere. It tried to open a warehouse, got things going and in six months or a year it fell apart. Nobody was opposed to ACOA per se, but the emphasis could be shifted somewhat to make it a more successful operation.
We should try to ensure that when the federal government attempts to do some work in a community there is a co-ordinated approach. I suspect, in many areas, that is just not the case.
Our caucus met just yesterday with representatives from the Sault and from Wawa about the work that they are doing. They are trying to pull together what sometimes seems like an incredible list of different agencies and particular federal agencies and actually try to deliver a service. That takes a major effort.
A couple of proposals that we have had are worth looking at. We think there is room for the federal government to move in this area. This government has some problems with the approach it is taking, but I do not think it should write some of these ideas off. I think they are good, positive ideas.
Two of our proposals are a community development fund and a single industry community fund. Under these proposals, funds would be provided to co-operative and community development corporations and other community-based initiatives. In the case of single industry towns, funding would also be made to assist those communities to explore diversification options.

A number of other comments were made. One of them is about public sector pension funds and where they are invested. So there are a number of experiments that have taken place in the country that obviously we can all learn from. But it is unfortunate that this government has really had some difficulty in trying to understand some proposals and projects.
In summary, this motion is an important one. It is important to get a message to this government about the concerns from Atlantic Canada. The few times that I have visited the area I have found the people to be absolutely wonderful. They are always more than pleased to discuss their concerns with people in responsible positions about the economy and what can be done. But a government that is aloof and not prepared to deal with things directly will never be of benefit to the maritimes.
We need some initiatives and opportunities from this government so that it does not just throw the maritimes on the trash heap like it is wont to do.
In conclusion, I would like to move an amendment. I have it right here for you to send up. I move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words following
the word fishery and adding the following thereto:
passenger and freight railway, forestry, shipbuilding and the post office and, further, that the premiers of the Atlantic provinces be condemned for their failure to fight Ottawa on behalf of their provinces.

This motion talks about the cut in the transfer payments to the Atlantic provinces. It threatens the stability of health care and education and creates destructive policy with regard to the fishery, railway and post office.
Since the debate began this morning I have been talking to my constituency office and to some constituents. They have great difficulty understanding how we on this side of the House can get up and say that the government has reduced payments and the hon. Minister of Finance this morning talked about increasing them.
If I could clarify that. I want to take one example. Indeed they have increased but not to the extent promised. If I could use some figures that were quoted for Newfoundland, the Minister of Finance said this morning that in 1984-85 the per capita transfer payments amounted to $1,617 per person. He went on in the same breath to say that seven years later, in 1991-92 it was $2,473. Well on the surface that sounds very good. It is over 50 per cent and I am still getting the figures. But I did a calculation based on some pamphlets that I read and to stay abreast of inflation alone in those seven years, you needed over $2,500. So the $2,473 did not keep those people who were relying on transfer payments abreast of inflation. In that interval of seven years they experienced 22 tax increases, plus a goods and services tax. So I would suggest that that $2,473 buying power is not $1,617 as it was seven years ago, but more like $1,300 or $1,400.
I am sure the minister did not do this deliberately, but when you hear it in a phrase you can draw some pretty poor conclusions from it and I want to make that clear.
The second point I want to make clear is that there was a formula for the Established Programs Financing, which was one of 14 ways of transferring money to the provinces. The EPF, which is the provinces' assistance in financing health services, extended health care and post-secondary education was calculated by an authority, the National Council on Welfare which was quoted by

Supply
my colleague from Gander-Grand Falls. It worked on changing the formula, which started in 1986. It started going with the economy. Then it was the economy minus two per cent. Then it was the economy minus three per cent and that was extended for two years, then for another five years and another three years beyond that.
The difference in those payments for which health and education rely on is $100 million in one year. The total from 1986 to 2000 is $100 billion for all of Canada. That is $100 billion less than it would have been if the formula had not been changed by the government.
That certainly clarifies the issue for me. Very simply, yes, they have increased the EPF but they have not kept up with inflation. It is a lot less than the provinces had expected.
In the case of Newfoundland, the minister said himself that the transfer payments make up 45.5 per cent of the total budget of Newfoundland. It used to be almost 49 per cent. It has gone down by many, many billions of dollars.
I want to talk also a little bit about the post office. A few years ago it was the plan of Canada Post to amalgamate, remove, change and replace 5,221 post offices that employ 10,000 people. In rural post offices 83 per cent of the employees are women.
We have in Newfoundland about 180 rural post offices, and they are being closed left, right and centre. If that was not bad enough, as again pointed out by my colleague, the head of Canada Post is getting a bonus of $100,000.
If you can tell me why that does not upset the people in my riding who see this from afar, by golly, Mr. Speaker, you would be a very understanding person. Let me tell you something else. I would like to create an image.
You are there in Newfoundland, and you are watching this happen. You are from the district of Port au Bras where a lot of fishing takes place, good professional fishermen as indeed in all the ridings.
They are watching foreigners take fish from a NAFO area that everybody in Newfoundland deserves: 3 November Oscar, 3NO. I have not got a track, but the northern edge of that NAFO area is 45 miles off the coast of Newfoundland. That is 45 miles. On a clear day, you can see the foreigners fishing from the capes on the Avalon Peninsula. They are fishing within our area. They
are taking our fish and our fishermen are not allowed to go out and fish there.
They decide: "Well, we are going to try it on for size anyway. We are so frustrated'. So, they go out and fish and the government sends the navy to go out and arrest our vessels when we know that foreigners are overfishing.
I am not simplifying that. Newfoundlanders are watching that and the government is asking: Why am I getting emotional? Why am I using language that is unbecoming to me?
All you have to do is be in my riding for 10 minutes. You would do an awful lot of things that are not becoming to you or anybody else of reasonable measure. With regard to railway, a few years ago the government said: "We got a deal for you. We are going to give you $800 million over 15 years".
The railway in Newfoundland was losing $50 million a year and in 15 years, that was $750 million. They said: "We are going to give you $800 million and we are going to give you some roads". On September 1, 1988, we lost the railroads. We did not get any roads, and the provincial government made $50 million on the deal. That is not a good deal at all.
What have I covered: rails, fishing, post office and the clarification of the transfer payments. There is one other area that has become a by-word with Atlantic Canadians, certainly Newfoundlanders. It does not matter what the Minister of Fisheries says, it does not matter what his parliamentary secretary says, it does not matter what the Prime Minister says. The fact of the matter is that in our opinion, we are the only country in the world that gives away the very resources upon which that part of Canada depends to foreigners, legally.
We give it to them legally and we know they are taking almost as much as we are allowing Newfoundlanders and Atlantic Canadians to catch illegally, but we send our destroyers out to arrest Canadian fishing vessels and bring them home. We do not get tangled up with foreigners, because the last time that happened I think we had some difficulties catching them when they went back to New Bedford.
I am not blaming that on the navy. What I am saying is that if you have something you want to enforce, why do you not target the foreigners, the ones we should be targeting. If you cannot do it with ships, try something else. I do not know, I am not the government. It should have the answers to that.

There is one other area while I am on the business of fishing and overfishing. I talked earlier about the Atlantic Catch Failure program. I really take objection to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans-my colleagues do as well-trying to create the impression that there is more than adequate money there and that the program is generous.
The phones in my riding have not stopped ringing for the last week. I can tell you there are 400 or 500 people in my riding alone who cannot qualify because there is not enough money.
In conclusion-I am going to wrap up-I do not often become emotional. I do not often use language or rhetoric in this House, but I am telling you that we have been moved in Atlantic Canada. We understand the difficulty the government has with the deficit. It seems that every time it moves its hand to initiate a policy, we get the dirty end of the stick. That is the perception.
If you relive the last 10 minutes that I have described to you, it would be difficult to have a perception other than that. So, I enjoin my colleagues from the other side of the House to have some feeling for the difficulty we are in, to show compassion and perhaps some imagination and creative thinking in trying to rectify this demoralizing and devastating situation of which we are speaking.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate today on a very important motion, one that was put forward by my party and one that concerns Atlantic Canada.
This motion condemns the government for reducing the level of transfer payments to Atlantic Canada because it will threaten the stability of health care and education and it also further condemns the government for its destructive policies toward the fishery, the railway and the post office.
My riding is Malpeque, Prince Edward Island. I want to say that in a small province like mine, reducing the level of transfer payments, as this government has done, has had a very devastating effect upon the whole economy. It is important that the federal government realize what a difficult position it has put my province in because of the reduction of transfer payments and the
Supply
other economic policies which this government has inflicted on Atlantic Canada.
I am not here this afternoon to condemn in whole the equalization formula and I am not advocating in any way that it be scrapped. But when you are dealing with a small province like Prince Edward Island, I think it is important that the federal government realize the difficult position that a small province like Prince Edward Island finds itself in because of the reduction of transfer payments.
We are talking about my province that operates with a total budget of a little over $700 million. We are talking about a province where the per capita income is 34 per cent below the average. This province that has undergone an estimated economic loss of $40 million to $50 million due to problems experienced by our potato industry as a result of this government's mishandling of the PVY-N potato crisis.
That is for the first year alone. It is anyone's guess what we will be losing this year.
We are also talking about a province that has lost nearly $100 million due to changes in federal payments made by this government since 1988. To take that $100 million and break it down, it means that $45 million of that has been in equalization payments and $54 has been in established program funding changes, changes to the EPF. As we know, that is the money that is given to the provinces to go to health and post-secondary education.
Just as important, we are talking about a region of the country that is faced with very high unemployment. The unemployment rate in my province is approximately 17 per cent. We have businesses in the country that are going under in record numbers. The bankruptcy rate in eastern Canada increased 14 per cent this past August.
Many of the problems I have mentioned are simply a result of the federal government's economic policy that has advocated high interest rates and a high dollar over the creation of jobs.
This week my province learned that expected revenues from the equalization payments would be reduced by another $17 million. The point that I want to make is not so much that Prince Edward Island will need to find an additional $17 million in an already tight budget. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it will be very difficult. The point that I want to make here is that my province, along with other regions of our country, has been placed in a

desperate situation by policies and past budgets of this government.
The latest shortfall of $17 million as I say will be hard to find in an already tight budget in Prince Edward Island. When you compare that with the $100 million that my province has lost by changes that this government has made to the established program funding and equalization payments since 1988, it may not seem that large. Given the current economic condition in my province, I could tell you that it will have a significant impact.
My province like many others is struggling to maintain its health care system. I know that many of my constituents have spoken to me about their concerns regarding the health care system, what this government is doing and about what this would mean down the road.
The minister of health and social services on Prince Edward Island has expressed his concern many times. I want to quote the Hon. Wayne Cheverie: "The reduction in the rate of increase and transfer payments is an attack on the basic foundation of our health care system. They represent drastic reductions of federal contributions that will have major consequences for the system of health care as we know it on Prince Edward Island".
That was the Minister of Health and Social Services. He along with all Islanders are really concerned about what the cuts in the transfer payments are going to mean to a small province like Prince Edward Island. Really we are seeing an example of these cuts already. We have already seen some hospital beds close and cuts to other services.
I know that my time is limited. I want to pass on to another area where these transfer payments are affecting and that certainly is education. This past fall the post-secondary students certainly felt the brunt of the cuts to the established programs funding as they were forced to pay higher tuition fees.
The president of the University of Prince Edward Island has expressed his concern about the dwindling government funding and he has indicated that this was the reason for the increase. He said: "Because of budget restraints and reductions in federal payments, the province increased UPEI's funding by only 4.1 per cent. The only thing we could do was raise tuitions".
That is a quote from Dr. Elliot who is the president of the University of Prince Edward Island and that is exactly what happened. They raised tuition fees by 15 per cent. Really what that means to each student is approximately $280 more for a 10-course term.
Mr. Speaker, you have indicated to me that my time is running out. I just want to make some closing remarks by calling on the government to recognize the damage that its policies has caused Atlantic Canadians, to recognize the devastating effect that they are having on the whole economy in the eastern part of Canada and also to ask the federal government to put forward its commitment that the level of transfer payments will not be further eroded by destructive policies like this government has advocated in the past.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning I would like to thank you for the obvious compliment you showed me. Obviously my diet is having an effect and I am wasting away to nothing.
I know the House waits with great interest for the remarks of my hon. friend from Egmont but with your indulgence I might make a brief intervention into the discussion here today. Needless to say I read with great interest the motion of my hon. friend from Gander-Grand Falls who I know has a great and longstanding
October 24, 1991

interest in Atlantic Canada issues. Elis omnibus motion seems to suggest that the government has done less than well by Atlantic Canada.
I do not know if that is the point he is trying to get across or not but obviously he has been missing a few things with respect to what has been going on in Atlantic Canada. I would like to share with him some of the perspectives and views that I might have on this.
I noticed that he begins by talking about transfer payments. I listened with interest to my hon. friend opposite with respect to transfer payments and higher education funding as it affected Prince Edward Island. I find it amazing that every time I come into this place and hear my hon. friends opposite, be they from the Liberal Party or the New Democratic Party, they always talk about ways that governments can spend money. They are a little less good at telling us what taxes should be raised or whether we should increase the deficit.
We know that our friends in the Liberal Party are real experts at increasing deficits because when they left power in 1984 they left a deficit of $38 billion and a national debt of $200 billion. These have compounded to being a $400 billion debt today. They left us a $16 billion operating deficit that this government, through wise and sound management, has transformed into a $12 billion operating surplus. Now that is performance.
When we talk about reducing the level of transfer payments in the Atlantic provinces what we are really talking about is government spending. My hon. friends opposite are all in favour of government spending, though they seem to ignore the fact that the only thing you spend is taxpayers' dollars. I want to tell him something, and it is that the message I am getting from many of the Atlantic Canadians that I know, including the 77,000 I have the privilege to represent here is that they do not want higher taxes. They have had enough of taxes. I have heard my hon. friends opposite complain about taxes. They have complained about tax reform which is one of the wise measures this government has introduced to tiy to have a more equitable and fair tax system and a tax system that is going to facilitate economic growth and development in this country.

It is only through taxation that we accrue the revenues that pay for all the wonderful things that my hon. friends opposite think we should have, including transfer payments, including for example the $800 million that is paid to the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada through unemployment insurance. I hear some of my friends from Atlantic Canada complain that this government is taking a great deal of interest in supporting our farmers in western Canada. We had an announcement a couple of weeks ago of $800 million of aid to western agriculture in a time of crisis. We forget that every year we put $800 million into our Atlantic fishery in support, not to mention the other financial supports that are provided to our fishery in Atlantic Canada.
As my hon. friend from Gander-Grand Falls knows, and I am sure he applauded the government and indeed this Minister of Fisheries of Oceans, when not two weeks ago he brought down a $39 million aid package in support of the Newfoundland fishing industry which has faced the most severe crisis in its history with the ice problem this year. But the government responded. This government is not afraid to spend money when it is necessary to assist and support Canadians, but this government believes in fiscal responsibility and, furthermore, it believes that those other levels of government that spend the public's money have a responsibility to be fiscally responsible as well.
So when this government brings in measures that cap transfer payments, though there is no cap on equalization which is so important to Atlantic Canada, there is no cap on the Canada Assistance Plan which is so important to Atlantic Canada and, of course, this government introduced the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency with a budget in excess of $1 billion to support economic development in Atlantic Canada, all those measures were introduced because they were necessaiy and supportive of Atlantic Canada.
Earlier today I heard my hon. friend from Halifax asking a question in the House about what this government was going to do to help Halifax. I thought it was a very commendable decision that this government made, not to mention a very' appropriate and proper decision that this government made, in placing the minesweeper

contract in the port of Halifax. It will mean $200 million of expenditure for Nova Scotia and for Halifax.
The government is prepared to spend money, but this government spends money frugally and wisely as it should, because every cent that is spent by government has to be accounted for because it comes from the taxpayers. I would urge my hon. friends opposite never to forget that.
My hon. friend from Gander-Grand Falls has recently been asking an awful lot of questions about expenditures by this government with respect to salaries of senior public servants and the heads of Crown corporations. I have got to tell him that he gets an awful lot of sympathy from this side of the House for some of those decisions. The one criticism that could perhaps be levelled at this government is that the system that it inherited from its predecessors which took back the two or three top levels of increments and made a bonus system. Unfortunately, it seems to have become a bonus system that is automatically paid, so my hon. friends opposite have been having a wonderful time looking at the fruits of the seeds that they planted when they set up that system so many years ago. I am sure my hon. friend from Gander-Grand Falls remembers it because he was a supporter of the government of the day that introduced that particular system.
When we talk about economic problems in Atlantic Canada, I think the first thing we have to recognize is that a good climate for economic growth is probably the thing that is going to help industry develop in Atlantic Canada better than anything else.
I look at my own constituency of South Shore, and I do not take anything away from any other part of Canada, but I must say there probably is no more beautiful place than the South Shore in Nova Scotia and there certainly no nicer place to live, to work and to make one's home. I look at one of the great accomplishments of this government with the free trade agreement which did not create that much change in tariff structures, but it guaranteed access to markets. I look at the constituency that I represent here and I look at the benefits that are accruing to my constituents because of that significant and important agreement.
Thke, for example, the Michelin tire plant in the town of Bridgewater which employs 1,500 people. Seventy per cent of the produce of that plant goes to the United States, 10 per cent goes to Japan and 20 per cent is sold to the rest of the market in Canada. Guaranteed access to the U.S. market is critically important to Michelin Tire.
I could mention the Christmas tree industry. My goodness, Mr. Speaker, though you would not know it on a warm day like today in Ottawa, but Christmas is approaching. If I may, I might just digress for a moment to remind all members of the House that as they look forward to celebrating Christmas this year they should think in terms of having a real Christmas tree, none of these phony artificial Christmas trees. I hope that you will take it up with the high officials in this place and the fire marshall to see that we enjoy the benefits of real Christmas trees right here in the House of Commons this year.
I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, and remind the House that on the south shore of Nova Scotia we export 1.25 million Christmas trees a year. Fifty per cent of the Christmas trees exported from this country are exported from the south shore of Nova Scotia. As you know, Lunenburg county is the Christmas tree capital of Canada. That is a $30 million business from the south shore of Nova Scotia, a business that is secured and guaranteed because of the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement.
Furthermore the duties have come down on Christmas tree rates. As a result we have seen a significant increase in the export of Christmas tree wreaths, so that the access we are guaranteed through the FTA to our Nova Scotia Christmas trees is another benefit of the FTA.
I could go on and talk about the pulp and paper industry. I could talk about the Bowater-Mersey Paper plant which, like all paper plants in the world right now are going through tough times. We could be in even tougher times if we did not know for sure that the 80 per cent of the paper that is produced in that mill has a guaranteed access into the United States market where the market is for that paper. The 800 people who work for Bowater-Mersey I am sure are very pleased that their future is secure in large measure because of the access provided in that agreement.

Or, of course, I could talk about our fishery. I could talk about the 8,500 people on the south shore who make their livelihood through the fishing industry either as harvesters or processors in one way or another and the fact that two-thirds of the fish that we produce go to the United States.
I guess what I am saying is that my hon. friends opposite said this was a heinous, terrible and villainous thing. On the other hand, it sure has guaranteed the future of the people on the south shore of Nova Scotia.
Now that is not to say that we have not been through difficult times. That is not to say that the downturn in the fishery, which has been caused by overfishing by Canadians and foreigners and by various other circumstances, has not hurt, has not meant plant closures. And I have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, and I know some of my hon. colleagues opposite have faced this, as have some of my colleagues on this side, there is nothing more difficult and challenging than to go to a one plant town the day they announce the plant is closing.
You know, I was in Lockeport two and a half years ago when they announced the closure of the National Sea Products plant. For two and a half years, under the leadership of an industrial adjustment service committee established under a program set up by the then minister of employment and immigration, the Canadian Jobs Strategy program, set that committee to work under the outstanding leadership of Mayor Mary Rose of Lockeport, working with provincial people and myself as a member. We have all worked together and we are going to continue to work until that plant reopens, which we hope is going to happen very soon.
It is the fact that the Government of Canada is open to responding to those kinds of problems that makes you hang in there and keep fighting.
I know my hon. friends from Newfoundland, I am sure, rejoiced this summer at the work that was done by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans when he put together deals and packages that reopened three major fish plants in Newfoundland. There was no partisan politics involved in that, because those fish plants were not all in ridings represented by government members. That is not the important thing. The important thing and the priority of this government is to look after the people. In this case we are talking about the people in communities in

Atlantic Canada, the same people that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans was concerned about when he brought in his ice aid package a couple of weeks ago. He is very sensitive to the needs of people in communities and that sort of thing.
My hon. friend's motion makes reference to the fishery. I might say we have had some very responsible leadership during difficult times in terms of trying to bring fisheries policy and the administration in the direction of the fishery and the fishery resource under control so that the maximum number of people can make a reasonable living in the fishery.
One of the harsh realities this government has faced is having to deal with a difficult financial situation. It could have run away from it and kept running the bills up as its predecessor did, but no, that is not its policy. It has tried to take control of the situation and bring it under control so that the country can grow, as it is starting to do again.
I see the IMF has predicted significant growth in the Canadian economy beyond the growth that is expected in the other G-7 countries. The government has done the same thing with respect to the fishery and bringing the fishery under control. They have increased enforcement measures, which has cut down significantly on cheating and other kinds of overfishing by our own fishermen.
They brought a helicopter into southwestern Nova Scotia. There was some concern expressed. I have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, I received a letter from the mayor of Yarmouth, Nova Scotia not so very long ago, and from the Chamber of Commerce in Yarmouth as well expressing concern that when the helicopter contract was up this March, it would not be renewed.
That helicopter has done a fantastic job of fisheries surveillance and it has done a wonderful job of air and sea rescue as well. It is a priority with everybody in southern Nova Scotia to see that contract renewed and see that helicopter remain there. It is an expensive thing, and the money has to be found.
Where there is a priority and people's needs and interests are in the forefront, this government responds. That is why I am confident that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Minister of Transport will work together and find the means whereby that helicopter will continue its stay in Yarmouth serving the people of that

October 24, 1991
Supply
area and in particular the fishermen who risk their lives every day going to sea.
We have heard a lot of talk from my hon. friend. He talks about the fishery, condemning the government for destructive policies. I notice he is frequently up in this Chamber talking about foreign vessels fishing in Canadian waters. I know, knowing my hon. friend as well as I do, it is certainly not his intention in any way to mislead anybody with respect to the issues that he raises.
I think it is very important that every single member of this House, and indeed Canadians, in particular Atlantic Canadians, understand where foreign vessels fish in the Atlantic fishery.
In 1973, the nations of the world that had an interest in the fishery and in the oceans of the world got together at the International Law of the Sea Conference and agreed that it was appropriate that coastal nations be allowed to declare a 200 mile economic fisheries control zone off their coasts.
Canada was one of the signatories to that agreement, but it was a voluntary agreement. The primary intent of that agreement was that it would give control of resources and particular fisheries resources to the adjacent state out beyond the continental shelf.
Except for three places in the world, 200 miles covers the limit out beyond the continental shelf. To our advantage or disadvantage, however you wish to describe it, the Grand Banks of Newfoundland are not one of those areas.
As I am sure you know, Mr. Speaker, because I know you have a great interest in the fishery, we have the nose and tail of the Grand Bank and the Flemish Cap sticking out beyond, and those areas are beyond Canada's international control. We have no right to tell anybody what to do in international waters.
Under that International Law of the Sea agreement, we are required to make available to other nations fisheries resources that we do not wish to harvest for ourselves in Canada. When we allow vessels from foreign countries to come inside our waters, we allow them to come in as we are required to do under the International Law of the Sea to harvest those resources that we have not been using.
Anybody who knows anything about fishing knows that when you put a hook or trawl line in the water, you are never 100 per cent sure what is going to come up and knows you have to have a by-catch.
I know my hon. friend from Gander-Grand Falls from time to time has had a great time talking about codfish allocations to these foreign nations when what he is really talking about are by-catches.
With a by-catch, one of the conditions that you can bring in, which is what this government did two years ago, is the condition that that by-catch has to be sold back for processing in Canadian plants so that in fact those fish do not go away from the plants where they could potentially create jobs for Canadians.
Similarly, I know my hon. friend talks about allocations of fish to the French, but something he never raises is the fact that before this government had the courage and the integrity to sit down and try to settle the 200 year old dispute with the French over the waters around St. Pierre and Miquelon that we had no idea how many fish they were taking.
The results of that now are that in fact there is less fish being taken now than there was before, but it is under control. As I am sure all members of the House are aware, we are awaiting the decision of the arbitration tribunal that will determine exactly where the lines are. We were fortunate enough to be able to use against the French the arguments that they themselves had used against the Channel Islands not so many years ago. It will be interesting to see. The important thing is that this government did not run away from the problem as its predecessor had done for years. It tackled the problem in the interests of Atlantic Canadians and in the interests of the Atlantic Canadian fishing industry.
One of the toughest problems we have yet to take on-and I know my friend from Gander-Grand Falls will be commenting on this-is taking on the challenge that we have too many people in his Province of Newfoundland-Labrador trying to make a living on too limited a resource in the fishery.
What do we do about that? I will be looking forward to hearing what he has to say about what his party proposes in solving that problem since he is suggesting that this government is not tackling those problems in a manner

that will have have long-term benefits for Atlantic Canada.
Do I sense, Mr. Speaker, that my time is winding down on me? I have many more comments I would like to make. Did I see you giving me the sign, or can I continue.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member just said a moment ago that there were too many fishermen in Newfoundland chasing too few fish.
The federal government announced two days ago that seven Japanese vessels would receive licences this year to catch tuna inside our 200 mile zone off his riding on the Scotia shelf. Does he not agree that foreign nations were given quotas this year inside Canada's 200 mile zone, in a meeting that took place in the hon. member's province? Under international agreement quotas were given for fish inside our 200 mile zone around Newfoundland, around Nova Scotia, to Bulgaria, Cuba, Denmark, including the Faro Islands and Greenland, to every country in the European Economic Community, to Japan, Norway, Poland, the U.S.S.R. and to another category called "others".

The only group there not allowed to come inside the 200 mile zone is the EEC. Does the hon. member not agree that before we start saying that there are too many Canadians chasing too few fish that first of all we should get rid of every single foreign fishing vessel in Canadian waters. I have seen him in action over in the Hague talking about foreign overfishing. I have seen him speak for three, four and five hours to those foreign nations, complaining about their fishing. Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to respond to those issues of my hon. friend because he has really just illustrated the point that I made in my general remarks, as I was confident he would.
First of all, I appreciate his raising the subject of our efforts on the other side of the ocean to persuade the Europeans to discontinue their destructive anti-environmental dangerous fishing effort outside Canada's 200 mile zone on the nose and tail of the Grand Bank. He knows perfectly well that one of the most destructive forces impacting negatively on northern Newfoundland is the destructive fishing that is going on by Spanish and Portuguese on the 2-J3KL cod stock outside, and on the flatfish stocks on the tail of the Grand Bank, primarily by Portuguese vessels. He knows that.
I am not sure whether he said I spoke eloquently, he said I spoke at length, but I must tell you that he and I were a great team over there, and contrary to what I have read in the press lately which suggested that he and I and others had other activities on our minds when we were over there-nonsensical stuff, by yellow-backed journalists-we were over there fighting for our fishermen as we should be. I agree 100 per cent with my hon. friend that not a single fish should be taken from within our waters by foreigners so long as we can get Canadians to go out there and fish it.
Now, when my hon. friend talks about allocations to foreign vessels to fish within our waters, you notice, my friends, that he neglected to mention what the quota allocations were that those vessels were getting. Did you

notice? I didn't notice his reference to that. Were they cod allocations, were they pollack allocations, were they haddock allocations? I don't recall his making any reference to that. My understanding of those allocations was that those allocations were from under-utilized stocks that we are not harvesting, things like silver hake and capelin.
I want to remind my hon. friend of the leadership that this government took, because this government has had a long-standing policy that we do not provide fisheries allocations to be bartered to foreigners. The previous Minister of Fisheries, now Minister of Employment and Immigration, in my judgment did a very courageous thing and he has been criticized roundly for it. He has been criticized in my constituency. I have had grief from plant owners and operators in my area over the allocations that that former Minister of Fisheries made in order to put the towns of Canso and Burgeo back into business again by making allocations of unused silver hake and capelin quotas so that they could be bartered for codfish from the Russians, which has put 500 people back to work in the town of Canso. That is decisive action by this government.
I might tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I am looking forward to this government doing the same thing for the community of Port Mouton. I have put a proposal before the Minister of Fisheries that would give us long-term allocations so that we can harvest those resources.
I will just finish on this point, Mr. Speaker, by saying that nobody is licensed to catch fish that Canadians are going to or are prepared to go and fish, nor should they be.

Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of the member's remarks he asked the rhetorical question: What taxes should be raised, as if taxes were always an outflow from the pockets of Canadians and were always a drain on them.
I would like to give the member an example of how using taxpayers' dollars, both in terms of loan guarantees as well as loans themselves and grants in the range of $5 million to a community, regrettably for the example not in Atlantic Canada, but in my riding, where that money ensured that the revenues of the province of Ontario, at $10 million a year, were maintained, and that revenues
for the federal government in the first year would be $16.5 million retained and $8.2 million thereafter, taxpayers' money.
I agree with him that it is taxpayers' money, not the government's money, although sometimes I think the government forgets that, which can be used to lever ongoing revenue to the federal and provincial treasuries. Should it not therefore be looked upon as an investment in the future of a community, a province or the country? I want to put it in the context of shipbuilding, particularly trawlers and what have you where we know that right now no trawlers are being built. It will take two or three years before from seven to nine a year are going to be built, but they cannot afford to have them built in Canada because of the high costs.
Would the hon. member not agree that we need to return to some form of level playing field internationally which means in the short term that we have got to match the kind of financial assistance offered to shipyards and to purchases of ships so that they can build them here at home instead of the reality today of almost 100 per cent of all shipyard work is government contracts?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend raises several very interesting points that I would like to comment on but obviously in one minute I cannot. I will briefly say this.
I agree with him 100 per cent on the use of loan guarantees. Canadians are fed up with free money being given to companies. Let us not forget that a loan guarantee still does tie up government funding that cannot be used for other things. Briefly, I agree with him totally on the use of loan guarantees and we need more of it.
On the shipbuilding industry, I think the secret to having a level playing field is for our shipbuilding companies to learn to be competitive. If we have too many shipbuilding companies, that is tough. We are faced with a fact that globally there are not a lot of ships being built. It is not just in Canada. Globally there are not a lot of ships being built, be they large fishing vessels which I think is what he is referring to, or other kinds of large ships. The question is: How can the Canadian government and how can the Canadian economy best
October 24, 1991

cope with the inevitable downsizing in the shipbuilding industry that is going to take place?
I think where we can become competitive over the next few years is not so much in new shipbuilding, but in attracting, as the Shelburne shipyard has done recently, Russian shipping vessels or foreign vessels for repair and maintenance work.
I look forward to pursuing the subject with my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, as has been stated before by many of my colleagues on this side of the House, we take no pleasure in speaking today in this debate. It seems that since 1988 we have had precious little economically or socially or constitutionally to brag about or be very positive about in this House of Commons.
I would just likely briefly refer to the previous speaker from South Shore. The reason we are having this debate today is because of the decrease in equalization payments to the Atlantic provinces. It is peculiar that the only Atlantic province that is receiving an increase in equalization payments this year is Nova Scotia, which means that basically Nova Scotia's economy has performed the worst over the past year.
If you listen to the member from South Shore you would think that because of the free trade agreement and everything else the economy in Nova Scotia was just booming. You would not really think he came from the same region as many of the previous speakers have come from and that is the Atlantic area. The figures show that he is definitely misleading or definitely giving the people of his province and the people of this House the wrong impression, that the economies of his riding and his province are doing well. Basically, the only reason his province is getting $1 million extra is because it has performed the worst of any province in Atlantic Canada.
Atlantic Canada is the region of the country that has by far the smallest population and within that region Prince Edward Island is by far the smallest province. Our small numbers and our limited resources and the seasonality of many of our industries make Atlantic Canada very vulnerable in these tough economic times, times of economic downturn.

One of the most distressing attitudes of this government is its obsession with the numbers game. If you do not have the numbers you just do not count. The human factor has been removed as a consideration when this government makes its decisions.
It is more interested in spending more millions of dollars trying to get credit for the few programs that remain in Atlantic Canada. For example in ACOA it spends millions of dollars in advertising and trying to take credit for itself for any programs that might be launched in the Atlantic area. It seems to put that emphasis on taking credit much more so than providing service to the region.
This government has become so bureaucratic and so legalistic in its approach that terms like compassion and social justice have disappeared from its vocabulary. They have been replaced with terms like cost recovery, bottom lines, user fees, rationalization and getting credit.
Many of our national institutions have been dismantled or are scheduled to be dismantled or are scheduled to be dismantled or have been privatized or scheduled to be privatized. We have a government that preaches national unity on the one hand and on the other it destroys the ties that have held this country together for well over 100 years.
In no place is this more true than in Atlantic Canada. Transportation, because of our location, is vital to our survival. It has been crippled by the policies of this government. It has become extremely difficult and extremely expensive for either people or goods to move within Atlantic Canada. It is also very difficult and very expensive to transport goods or people in or out of Atlantic Canada. The transportation problem alone puts us at a severe disadvantage.
When we combine it with other government policies in the region, we as Canadians are left to wonder about the real intentions and agenda of this government. We are left to wonder about the real effects of this government's decentralization policies. We are left to wonder about whether all Canadians are really equal in the eyes of this government. We are left to wonder if people are really a priority any more or are we being ruled by a corporate agenda.

This country has been in existence for over 123 years. In that time we have built a country that provides its residents with a standard of living, a quality of life that is the envy of the world. These standards and our quality of life are weakening rapidly. We have shown the world the benefits of unity. We, as Canadians, have reaped the benefits of unity. It is bitterly ironic that in the face of all of this we are now going through the worst unity crisis in our history.
It is a unity crisis that is sorely aggravated by our economic problems. Nowhere is this more true than in the Atlantic provinces. Our region is plagued by problems in every major economic sector; the fishery, agriculture, tourism. Atlantic governments have recognized how imperative it is that people who have common interests and common needs join together in common cause if they hope to make legitimate progress. They have made substantial moves toward economic unity and have plans to continue in this vein.
However, federal budgeting and legislative policies have made it very difficult for Atlantic governments to even maintain standards let alone improve them. A case in point is the recent federal decision to further reduce equalization payments by over $100 million.
While the press release issued by the premiers after their emergency meeting indicates they took the latest blow with some degree of equanimity, I must report that the people in my riding, and these are the only ones I have heard from to this point, are extremely concerned. They see a $50 million deficit for this province for this year. They know that this cannot continue and they know that something has to be done about it. They see more problems coming. There have to be cuts and the people know there have to be cuts.
The three main industries in my riding are fishing, agriculture, and tourism. The people in these industries have already been hammered by changes and difficulties beyond their control: the fishermen by changed carapace size, lower catches, and lower prices; the farmer by the potato virus and low beef and hog prices; the tourist operator by the GST inflated costs and a recession that has kept many tourists away. The effects of Bill C-21, changes to the UI Act, are starting to be felt. They fear more hard times are on the way and definitely they are right.
I want to emphasize that we are all aware of the hard times.
We are all aware of the deficit and we are all aware that we must do our share and we are willing to do our share. However, at this point we feel that a disproportionately high proportion of the burden has been shouldered by Atlantic Canada. We do not feel that we should be asked to carry more. Indications are, however, that this is exactly what is going to happen.
We were worried about the potential impact that constitutional change and the free trade agreement would have on programs such as health care. Now it looks like we will not have to wait for constitutional change as freezes and cutbacks are going to force changes right now.
People in my riding are looking at the health care system, medicare. Many are alarmed at what they see. We have already seen staff layoffs in hospitals. We have seen beds closed down. We have seen services curtailed. Now people see more of the same and these cuts are probably going to be permanent or are going to remain for quite a number of years.
People have reason to be concerned. They see this government cutting, cutting, cutting. They know that the capacity to deliver programs will be reduced because of these cuts. They know that people in our region will likely not be able to enjoy the same standard of health care as their fellow Canadians in more well-to-do provinces. For example, the Established Programs Financing program has been capped at 3 per cent. Health services in Prince Edward Island are increasing at the rate of 7 per cent which leaves a 4 per cent shortfall every year, year after year after year. How is Prince Edward Island going to be able to deliver the same level of services as British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario and Quebec?
Mr. Speaker, you have indicated that my time is almost up so thank you very much.

Mr. Speaker, I did not want to pass up on the opportunity of asking the member a little question given that it is small business week. Although the debate does not specifically centre around that particular aspect of it, I think that when we talk about rural post offices, when we talk about fisheries and when we talk about railroads and we talk about cutbacks in transfer payments to our Atlantic provinces, we are talking about a broader
October 24, 1991

community than just those directly affected by these moves.
Specifically, I would suggest that through the cut in transfer payments to the Atlantic provinces, what we are doing is either cutting massively on services that will hurt our seniors and others, particularly lower and middle income earners, or we will have to see the increase in taxes in the area and taxes come out of the pockets of the middle class and the small business community.
My question to the hon. member is, given the fact of these cuts, given the fact of what will be looked at, does he have any suggestions to the people of Atlantic Canada, and certainly to those of us in the rest of Canada, who have already faced some of these cuts, as to what the small business community in his area will think of these cuts and how it will think of this particular government giving those cuts and what is going to happen to it in the future?

Mr. Speaker, for the information of the hon. member, this is our second round of cuts. We have already gone through one round and this is our second kick at the cat in this regard. The less money that is in the province, the less money people have to spend and the less money will be spent in the small business sector of our province.
There is another thing I would like to mention that has been happening in Prince Edward Island, and I assume the same thing is happening in the member's own riding. The unemployment insurance program is a vital program for Atlantic Canada and especially Prince Edward Island where most of the main industries like tourism, agriculture and fisheries are seasonal industries and the majority of our work force is engaged in this three industries.
For the first time, with the fishing and tourism season being concluded, we see people going in to apply for unemployment insurance and they are faced with this particular questionnaire. It is called the insurable employment questionnaire. It says: "Complete and return with your application". The first question on this paper is: "Are you related to any of your employers by blood, marriage, including common law or adoption?" Then they go on to ask: "Do you have a controlling interest in any of the companies in which you have worked" and "are you involved in any business relationship with the employer?"

In areas of a small province such as Egmont in western Prince Edward Island, and especially in the fishing industry, very many of the employer and employees are related. It seems as if it is almost a crime to work for someone who happens to be your third, fourth or fifth cousin. It seems to be a crime to work even if your wife has a business and you as her husband are working in that particular business. This was never a problem in the past. In fact most of the recent court rulings have said there is absolutely nothing wrong with this particular employee and employer relationship.
If the applicant checks the "yes" block, then his form has to go to Revenue Canada and this tacks two, three or four weeks on to their waiting period. Instead of waiting for four weeks to have a claim processed to get money, which will then be circulated in the community, they have to wait almost two months.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak on this motion today. As my colleague from Egmont has said, we in Atlantic Canada do not get a great deal of pleasure in speaking on this particular subject. It indicates that the people in our area are not as successful as we would like and that we have economic difficulties which we want to improve upon.
We have a very difficult economic situation in Atlantic Canada. I would like to say that we in the opposition are working hand in hand with the government to try to find these answers. But that is not the case. The government maintains that everything is going well in Atlantic Canada. It has backed away from the problems that Atlantic Canadians are experiencing at the present time.
This motion talks about three areas in particular which are fundamental to the problems in Atlantic Canada. They are not the only problems. If we were to list every problem we would not have time for the debate. It would take from now until Christmas to debate the inconsiderate attitude of this government toward Atlantic Canada.
I think my colleagues have stated quite well the problems that exist, particularly the questions on fisheries, equalization and transfer payments. These are problems that the government just will not change its course on. The fishery is just devastated. There are no groundfish available to catch and, if there are, they are
